title: 03-Assistant Attorney General's Report
text: ASSISTANT ATTORNEY GENERAL’S REPORT January 22, 2026 1. Sullivan, et al., v. Summers, et al., No. 1:24-CV-00172 (D. Md.). Katherine Strauch Sullivan and David Morsberger, two registered voters from Maryland, filed suit against SBE in the federal district court in Maryland alleging that the Board’s current regulation defining “electoral process” for voter registration list purposes violates the National Voter Registration Act and First Amendment. The complaint, filed January 18, 2024, seeks declaratory and injunctive relief restricting enforcement of the regulation. On March 8, 2024, OAG filed a motion to dismiss on behalf of SBE. The plaintiffs filed a response in opposition on March 29, 2024. OAG filed a final reply on April 12, 2024. On August 30, 2024, plaintiffs filed a motion for summary judgment on a stipulated set of facts. OAG replied in opposition to the motion on September 13, 2024. The plaintiffs filed a reply to that opposition on September 23, 2024. On March 4, 2025, the district court issued a memorandum opinion and order granting plaintiffs’ motion as to Count I; and, denying SBE’s motion as to Count I. The court ruled that the regulation is preempted by the National Voter Registration Act. The parties were also ordered to file a status report on their positions relating to the remaining counts. On March 28, 2025, the parties filed a joint status report requesting the court dismiss the outstanding claims. The Court dismissed the outstanding claims, and issued a final judgment on Count I, on October 30, 2025. On November 13, 2025, plaintiffs filed a motion requesting attorneys’ fees. The parties thereafter negotiated a settlement agreement for the payment of attorneys’ fees. That agreement, which has been executed by the parties, will be submitted to the Board of Public Works for final approval. 2. Brian Della Rocca v.

The plaintiff served the suit on Secretary Lee and Chairperson Summers on January 16, 2025. OAG filed a motion to dismiss the suit on behalf of both state officials on February 6, 2025. Plaintiff opposed the motion; OAG filed a reply to the opposition on March 5, 2025. Mass)- On April 3, 2025, nineteen states, including Maryland, filed a civil complaint in the federal district court for the District of Massachusetts against the President, the United States Attorney General, the Election Assistance Commission, and the United States Secretary of Defense. The complaint alleges, amongst seven counts, that the Executive Order imposing certain requirements on the conduct of voter registration and federal elections is unlawful. On April 23, 2025, the defendants moved to consolidate the lawsuit with a second set of lawsuits filed in Washington D.C. that challenged the executive order. The court denied that motion on May 9, 2025. On May 5, 2025, the plaintiff states asked the court for a preliminary injunction to pause implementation of provisions of the Executive Order while the lawsuit was pending. The court granted the preliminary injunction after a hearing. The defendants have appealed the grant of the preliminary injunction to the First Circuit. Separately, on June 13, 2025, the defendants moved to dismiss the complaint. The plaintiff states filed a response in opposition on July 11, 2025. The Court conducted a hearing on the motion on September 4, 2025. On September 17, the Court issued a memorandum opinion and order denying the motion to dismiss.

title: 03-Assistant Attorney General's Report
text: C-02-CV-25-001586 (Cir. Ct. Anne Arundel County). On June 2, 2025, five registered voters unaffiliated with a political party in Maryland served a civil action on the Governor and State Board of Elections. The suit alleges that the registered voters’ electoral rights, granted by the Maryland Constitution, are violated by their inability to vote in state-run, partisan, primary elections. The voters accordingly seek declaratory judgment and an injunction preventing the State from “conducting, organizing or funding State primary elections in which unaffiliated voters are prohibited from voting.” OAG filed a motion to dismiss the complaint on July 30, 2025. Plaintiffs filed an opposition to the motion on August 29, 2025. A hearing on the motion took place on October 20, 2025. On November 14, 2025, the Court granted the motion, dismissing the case in a memorandum opinion. Plaintiffs have appealed the case to the Appellate Court of Maryland. On January 12, 2026, the unaffiliated voters filed a petition for a writ of certiorari in the Supreme Court of Maryland. The petition asks the Supreme Court to hear the appeal now, rather than waiting to potentially entertain the appeal after a judgment by the Appellate Court of Maryland. OAG is presently drafting an answer to the petition, which is due to the Supreme Court on or before January 27, 2026. January 22, 2026 Assistant Attorney General’s Report 6. The United States of America v. Jared DeMarinis, No. 1:25-CV-03934 (D. Md.) On December 3, 2025, the United States Department of Justice filed suit against the State Administrator of Elections over his response to the department’s multiple demands to disclose Maryland’s unredacted voter registration database. The complaint alleges that the State is in violation of a provision of the Civil Rights Act of 1960 in declining to hand over the unredacted information, as demanded.

title: 03-Assistant Attorney General's Report
text: The complaint alleges that the State is in violation of a provision of the Civil Rights Act of 1960 in declining to hand over the unredacted information, as demanded. With the complaint, DOJ filed a motion to compel records pursuant to the Civil Rights Act of 1960. The motion advocates to dispense with normal process and the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, and instead (in a summary fashion) compel production of the voter database. By agreement between the parties, OAG must file a response to both the complaint and the motion on or before January 30, 2026. 7. Republican National Committee, et al. v. Jared DeMarinis, et al., No. 1:25- CV-03989 (D. Md.) On December 5, 2025, the national and state entities of the Republican Party and two Republican voters registered in Maryland sued the State Administrator of Elections, State Board, and the local boards of elections for Montgomery and Howard County. The complaint alleges that election officials in Maryland are violating the National Voter Registration Act (“NVRA”) by failing to make reasonable efforts to remove ineligible voters from the voter registration database. In support of that allegation, the complaint cites estimated population statistics and compares them to SBE’s reported voter registration totals. On January 12, 2026, the Democratic National Committee moved to intervene in the case as a defendant. The plaintiffs did not oppose the motion to intervene. OAG, on behalf of SBE, took no position on the motion. The motion remains pending before the Court. By agreement between the parties, OAG must file a response to the complaint on or before January 30, 2026. January 22, 2026 Assistant Attorney General’s Report

A.-B. (text unchanged) C. Requirements for Training Compensation. (1) A local board shall pay at least $50 to an election judge who completes the training program[.], and serves as an election judge in the election for which the training was offered. (2) If the training program includes a training class that is offered through virtual instruction or online delivery and a hands-on practice session, the election judge shall complete the hands-on practice session to be entitled to compensation. (3) An election judge who is required to complete a training program prior to both a primary and general election is entitled to compensation for each training program,so long as the election judge serves as an election judge in the election for which the training was offered. Explanation: This regulation implements HB586, enacted in 2025, requiring election judges to work during the voting period to earn pay for training.

text: Participants in Address Confidentiality Programs. Subject to notification to the State or a local board of participation in the program described in § 3–2403 of the Courts and Judicial Proceedings Article, or the program described in § 7-303 of the State Government Article, an individual’s information shall be designated as confidential. [E]F. (text unchanged) .03 Applications A. (text unchanged) B. Form. (1) A person seeking to keep the person's residence address, telephone number, and email address of a record confidential shall apply in writing on a form approved by the State Administrator. (2) The form shall be filed: (a) At the appropriate local board if the applicant wishes to keep the applicant's residence address, telephone number, and email address provided on a voter registration application confidential; or, (b) At the State or local board at which the applicant filed the certificate of candidacy or statement of organization if the applicant wishes to keep the applicant's residence address, telephone number, or email address provided on a certificate of candidacy or statement of organization confidential. (3) A person seeking confidentiality need not complete the form if: (a) A person is a participant in the program described in § 3–2403 of the Courts and Judicial Proceedings Article, and the Administrative Office of the Courts notifies the State Board; or (b) A person is a participant in the program described in § 7-303 of the State Government Article, and the Secretary of State notifies the State Board. text: C. (text unchanged) .04 Consideration of Request A. Discretion Required. title: Policy 2025-03 PSR Request Policy
text:
Jared DeMarinis Michael Summers, Chairman
State Administrator
Jim Shalleck, Vice Chairman
Diane Butler
Katherine Berry
Deputy Administrator Victoria Jackson-Stanley
Policy 2025-03 PSR Request Policy
It is the policy of the State Board of Elections to administer and maintain voter registration
records accurately and transparently. In doing so, the State Board must balance the requirements
for public disclosure of registration records imposed by laws like Election Law § 3-505 against
voters’ privacy interest in the personally identifying information they provide for registration. No
one should be dissuaded from registering to vote because of the fear of identity theft or
unwarranted intrusion into their private life.
Therefore, the State Board of Elections provides the following policy for disclosure of voter
registration applications pursuant to public information requests.
The following information should be redacted from disclosure before any registration
application is released publicly:
1. Maryland Driver’s License Number
2. Social Security Number
3. Personal Phone Number
4. Personal Email Address
5. Agency through which the Voter Registered or Updated their Registration
All other information contained in the voter registration application may be disclosed
without redaction.
All PSR requests that are countywide or by district requests will be charged $75 and
statewide data requests will be charged $125. Individual record requests will be charged as a
countywide request after 2 hours of data gathering has occurred for a requester that sends
multiple requests.

title: Policy 2025-04 Election Judge Parity Reporting
text:
Jared DeMarinis Michael Summers, Chairman
State Administrator
Jim Shalleck, Vice Chairman
Diane Butler
Katherine Berry
Deputy Administrator Victoria Jackson-Stanley
Policy 2025-04 Election Judge Parity Reporting
Pursuant to Election Law Article §10-201, the Election Director shall assign election judges to
achieve parity to the extent practicable at each polling place. In order to assist in the recruitment
of election judges, the Election Director shall provide a vacancy report monthly to their local
board of elections members beginning in February 2026. The vacancy report should be a
statistical report which includes the polling place and party breakdown by election judge type.

title: 2026-02-19 AAG report
text: ASSISTANT ATTORNEY GENERAL’S REPORT February 19, 2026 1. Sullivan, et al., v. Summers, et al., No. 1:24-CV-00172 (D. Md.). Katherine Strauch Sullivan and David Morsberger, two registered voters from Maryland, filed suit against SBE in the federal district court in Maryland alleging that the Board’s current regulation defining “electoral process” for voter registration list purposes violates the National Voter Registration Act and First Amendment. The complaint, filed January 18, 2024, seeks declaratory and injunctive relief restricting enforcement of the regulation. On March 8, 2024, OAG filed a motion to dismiss on behalf of SBE. The plaintiffs filed a response in opposition on March 29, 2024. OAG filed a final reply on April 12, 2024. On August 30, 2024, plaintiffs filed a motion for summary judgment on a stipulated set of facts. OAG replied in opposition to the motion on September 13, 2024. The plaintiffs filed a reply to that opposition on September 23, 2024. On March 4, 2025, the district court issued a memorandum opinion and order granting plaintiffs’ motion as to Count I; and, denying SBE’s motion as to Count I. The court ruled that the regulation is preempted by the National Voter Registration Act. The parties were also ordered to file a status report on their positions relating to the remaining counts. On March 28, 2025, the parties filed a joint status report requesting the court dismiss the outstanding claims. The Court dismissed the outstanding claims, and issued a final judgment on Count I, on October 30, 2025. On November 13, 2025, plaintiffs filed a motion requesting attorneys’ fees. The parties thereafter negotiated a settlement agreement for the payment of attorneys’ fees.

February 19, 2026 Assistant Attorney General’s Report Thereafter, the proceedings were stayed at the government’s request due to the lapse in appropriations for the Department of Justice. That stay lifted when appropriations were reallocated to the Department. On Friday, December 12, 2025, the parties filed cross-motions for summary judgment. OAG worked with SBE to provide a factual declaration on Maryland’s behalf in support of the plaintiff-states’ motion for summary judgment. 4. California, et al., v. Trump, et al., 1:25-CV-010810 (1st Cir.)- This is the appeal of the preliminary injunction granted in the above matter. On October 7, 2025, the Government filed appellants’ brief. However, soon after, the proceedings were stayed at the government’s request due to the lapse in appropriations for the Department of Justice. That stay lifted when appropriations were reallocated to the Department. The case is now fully briefed. 5. Serena Bryson, et al., v. Westley Moore, et al., No. C-02-CV-25-001586 (Cir. Ct. Anne Arundel County). On June 2, 2025, five registered voters unaffiliated with a political party in Maryland served a civil action on the Governor and State Board of Elections.

title: 2026-02-19 AAG report
text: That stay lifted when appropriations were reallocated to the Department. The case is now fully briefed. 5. Serena Bryson, et al., v. Westley Moore, et al., No. C-02-CV-25-001586 (Cir. Ct. Anne Arundel County). On June 2, 2025, five registered voters unaffiliated with a political party in Maryland served a civil action on the Governor and State Board of Elections. The suit alleges that the registered voters’ electoral rights, granted by the Maryland Constitution, are violated by their inability to vote in state-run, partisan, primary elections. The voters accordingly seek declaratory judgment and an injunction preventing the State from “conducting, organizing or funding State primary elections in which unaffiliated voters are prohibited from voting.” OAG filed a motion to dismiss the complaint on July 30, 2025. Plaintiffs filed an opposition to the motion on August 29, 2025. A hearing on the motion took place on October 20, 2025. On November 14, 2025, the Court granted the motion, dismissing the case in a memorandum opinion. Plaintiffs have appealed the case to the Appellate Court of Maryland. On January 12, 2026, the unaffiliated voters filed a petition for a writ of certiorari in the Supreme Court of Maryland. The petition asks the Supreme Court to hear the appeal now, rather than waiting to potentially entertain the appeal after a judgment by the Appellate Court of Maryland. OAG filed an answer to the petition on January 27, 2026. February 19, 2026 Assistant Attorney General’s Report 6. The United States of America v. Jared DeMarinis, No. 1:25-CV-03934 (D.Md.) On December 3, 2025, the United States Department of Justice filed suit against the State Administrator of Elections over his response to the department’s multiple demands to disclose Maryland’s unredacted voter registration database.

title: 2026-02-19 AAG report
text: February 19, 2026 Assistant Attorney General’s Report 6. The United States of America v. Jared DeMarinis, No. 1:25-CV-03934 (D.Md.) On December 3, 2025, the United States Department of Justice filed suit against the State Administrator of Elections over his response to the department’s multiple demands to disclose Maryland’s unredacted voter registration database. The complaint alleges that the State is in violation of a provision of the Civil Rights Act of 1960 in declining to hand over the unredacted information, as demanded. With the complaint, DOJ filed a motion to compel records pursuant to the Civil Rights Act of 1960. The motion advocates that the Court must dispense with normal process and the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and instead must, in a summary fashion, simply compel production of the voter database. By agreement between the parties, OAG filed a motion to dismiss and an opposition to the motion to compel on January 30, 2026. Two intervening defendants also filed motions to dismiss and oppositions to the motion to compel on the same date. DOJ filed a consolidated response to all the defendants’ filings on February 13, 2026. The defendants may file a final reply on or before February 27, 2026. 7. Republican National Committee, et al. v. Jared DeMarinis, et al., No. 1:25- CV-03989 (D.Md.) On December 5, 2025, the national and state entities of the Republican Party and two Republican voters registered in Maryland sued the State Administrator of Elections, State Board, and local boards of elections for Montgomery and Howard County. The complaint alleges that election officials in Maryland are violating the National Voter Registration Act (“NVRA”) by failing to make reasonable efforts to remove eligible voters from the voter registration database.

title: 2026-02-19 AAG report
text: The complaint alleges that election officials in Maryland are violating the National Voter Registration Act (“NVRA”) by failing to make reasonable efforts to remove eligible voters from the voter registration database. In support of that allegation, the complaint cites estimated population statistics and compares them to SBE’s reported voter registration totals. On January 12, 2026, The Democratic National Committee moved to intervene in the case as a defendant. The plaintiffs (RNC, Md. GOP, and voters) did not oppose the motion to intervene. OAG, on behalf of SBE, took no position on the motion. The motion remains pending before the Court. OAG filed a motion to dismiss the complaint on January 30, 2026. The local boards of elections, through their counsel, also filed motions to dismiss on the same date. On February 2, 2026, the Court granted the pending motion to intervene, permitting the DNC to participate in the case as a defendant. February 19, 2026 Assistant Attorney General’s Report By agreement between the parties, the plaintiffs will file a consolidated response to the motions to dismiss on or before March 13, 2026. The defendants may then file replies on or before April 17, 2026. February 19, 2026 Assistant Attorney General’s Report

text: Phone Texting Commands VOTE HELP Text to 77788 Text to 77788  Register To Vote  Additional information CHECK Text to 77788  Review your voter registration  Find out where to vote  Find out your voting districts  See the status of your mail-in or provisional ballot UPDATE Text to 77788  Update your voter registration VBM Text to 77788  Apply To Vote By Mail BOX Zip Code Text + to 77788 Example: BOX 20879  Ballot Drop Box and Post Office Locator EV Zip Code Text + to 77788 Example: EV 20879  Three Nearby Early Voting Centers  Wait Times SERVE to 77788 Text  Serve as an Election Worker 8 Choose How To Vote In Person 9 Election Security Our Voting Equipment Is Not Connected to the Internet Neither the Ballot Marking Device nor the digital scanner that counts your ballot is ever connected to the Internet. Each scanner has been certified by the U.S. Election Assistance Commission. The Montgomery County Board of Elections tests every scanner to ensure that it counts accurately before sending it to the polls. The Montgomery County Board of Elections follows strict chain of custody procedures and audit results after Election Day to make sure the scanners were not tampered with. Backup Systems Are in Place to Protect Election Results There are several backup systems in place to protect the validity of election results. First, results are printed on paper at each polling place. Second, a digital scan of each ballot is stored on a removable drive. Third, the paper ballots themselves can be used in an audit or recount, as they were during the 2018 and 2022 primary election recounts. There are also backup systems for voter registration.

title: MoCo Voter Guide for the 2026 Primary Election 02062026
text: First, results are printed on paper at each polling place. Second, a digital scan of each ballot is stored on a removable drive. Third, the paper ballots themselves can be used in an audit or recount, as they were during the 2018 and 2022 primary election recounts. There are also backup systems for voter registration. Notices are mailed to voters for every change, and each polling place has a paper list of voters. Anyone who disputes his or her voter registration can cast a provisional ballot, and election officials will determine after Election Day whether the ballot was validly cast and will be counted. We Are Looking Out for Your Safety A dedicated bipartisan team of professionals and volunteers preserve the chain of custody of your ballot and the voting data. All employees receive background checks and thousands of election workers of different party affiliations work together to ensure election integrity. The safety and security of election workers and voters is our priority, and we continuously work and coordinate with the Montgomery County Police Department and other relevant agencies to provide a safe voting experience. Election Results Are Not Confirmed Immediately, and Mail-In Ballots and Provisional Ballots Continue to Be Counted AFTER Election Day The results reported and any races called by the media on election night are not final. The election will not be certified for at least two weeks after Election Day, until all Mail-in and provisional ballots are counted. This allows time to audit the results, investigate complaints, and make sure every vote counts. If you return your Mail-in ballot early, it will be processed before Election Day.

title: MoCo Voter Guide for the 2026 Primary Election 02062026
text: The election will not be certified for at least two weeks after Election Day, until all Mail-in and provisional ballots are counted. This allows time to audit the results, investigate complaints, and make sure every vote counts. If you return your Mail-in ballot early, it will be processed before Election Day. Election officials will start processing received ballots on Monday, June 1, but no results are tabulated before the polls open at 7AM on Election Day, Tuesday June 23, nor released until the polls close that day at 8PM. Montgomery County may take longer to announce final results because there are more voters, usually more Mail-in ballots, and more print-your-own Internet-delivered ballots (that must be hand-duplicated) than in other Maryland counties. All validly cast ballots will be counted, whether or not they will change the results. VOTING ACCESSIBILITY Voters With Disabilities Maryland’s Voting System offers features for accessibility. Please ask the Election Judge about your options. At least one touchscreen ballot marking device will be available at each site with large-print, high contrast, Braille, and audio capabilities. Each ballot marking device has a keypad that allows voters with visual impairments to navigate the ballot and make their choices. Language Access As required by Section 203 of the Voting Rights Act of 1975, the ballot marking device offers both visual and audio instructions in either English or Spanish as selected by the voter. Interpreters are available to assist voters who speak Spanish while additional language assistance options are available to speakers of other languages determined by the State Board of Elections through the new Language Assistance Program. The Board of Elections is committed to serving all County voters, including limited-English speakers.

title: MoCo Voter Guide for the 2026 Primary Election 02062026

Poll workers are trained and have access to various language resources to assist with communication in Amharic, Chinese, French, Korean, Spanish, Vietnamese, and other languages. 10 ELECTION WORKERS NEEDED! An election judge is a registered Maryland voter who volunteers to assist voters during early voting and on Election Day. The role of an election judge is to ensure fair and accessible elections for all voters and to protect the integrity of the election process. • Due to the diversity of languages spoken within the County, bilingual election judges are needed. • Election Judges who are fluent in both English and Spanish are especially needed in each polling place to meet the requirements of Section 203 of the 1975 Voting Rights Act and the Language Assistance Program established by Title 15.5 of the Maryland Election Law Article. • Election workers will earn a minimum $250 stipend per full day. If you served at a polling place during the 2024 elections, you also will receive a $100 bonus per full day served ($50 for half-day shifts) during early voting and on Election Day. It is the policy of the State Board of Elections to administer and maintain voter registration
records accurately and transparently. In doing so, the State Board must balance the requirements
for public disclosure of registration records imposed by laws like Election Law § 3-505 against
voters’ privacy interest in the personally identifying information they provide for registration.
PIA
The State Board of Elections provides the following PIA policy for disclosure of voter
registration applications pursuant to public information requests.
The following information should be redacted from disclosure before any registration
application is released publicly:
1. Maryland Driver’s License Number
2. Social Security Number
3. Personal Phone Number
4. Personal Email Address
5. Agency through which the Voter Registered or Updated their Registration
All other information contained in the voter registration application may be disclosed without
redaction. Individual records requests will be charged as a countywide request after 2 hours of data
gathering has occurred for a requester that sends multiple requests (see PSR below).
PSR
All PSR requests that are countywide or by district requests will be charged $75 and statewide
data requests will be charged $125.

title: State Certification Testing for Voting Systems 2026- 2.9.2026
text: State Certification Testing for Voting Systems Maryland State Board of Elections F ebruary 2026 V2.0 State Certification Testing for Voting Systems Introduction This document describes the requirements for vendors seeking state certification for voting systems. The State Board of Elections (SBE) will conduct all testing independently of the voting system vendor. The testing results, along with a recommendation by the State Administrator, will be presented to the members of the State Board of Elections who, during a publicly held State Board Meeting, will formally vote on whether the voting system will be certified. If the voting system includes a certified network component and an uncertified election night network component, only the portion of the voting system related to the certified network will be considered by the members of the State Board of Elections for certification. However, SBE will make a recommendation to the board based on the viability of the entire system which would include all components certified and otherwise. Please note, if SBE is going through an active procurement for a new voting system, only the system selected will go through the Maryland State Certification testing. Overview 1) Timeline – 60 days 2) Application a) Identification of System. The application shall specify clearly the specific equipment, hardware, firmware, and software for which certification is sought. b) Overview of System. The application shall provide a brief overview description of the voting system. Marketing brochures may be used for this purpose. c) Use in Other Jurisdictions.

The application shall include a list of all jurisdictions where: i) The exact system for which certification is being sought, or a model or version of the system is in use, together with: (1) The price that was charged to the jurisdiction for the system, and (2) A breakdown of the per unit price and the price of any components. ii) The exact system for which certification is being sought, or a model or version of the system has been but is no longer in use; and iii) A request has been made for approval of the exact system for which certification is being sought or a model or version of the system, together with a statement of whether the request was granted, was denied, was withdrawn, or is pending. d) Qualification Certificate. If an independent testing laboratory has completed qualification testing on the voting system, the application shall be accompanied by a: i) Copy of the qualification certificate issued for the voting system; and ii) Signed authorization directing the independent testing laboratory that performed the qualification testing to: (1) Submit the results of its testing directly to the evaluation agent; and (2) Allow the evaluation agent or his or her designee full access to all test records and data. e) Certification Testing Transfer.

text: C-02-CV-25-001586 (Cir. Ct. Anne Arundel County). On June 2, 2025, five registered voters unaffiliated with a political party in Maryland served a civil action on the Governor and State Board of Elections. The suit alleges that the registered voters’ electoral rights, granted by the Maryland Constitution, are violated by their inability to vote in state-run, partisan, primary elections. The voters accordingly seek declaratory judgment and an injunction preventing the State from “conducting, organizing or funding State primary elections in which unaffiliated voters are prohibited from voting.” March 26, 2026 Assistant Attorney General’s Report OAG filed a motion to dismiss the complaint on July 30, 2025. Plaintiffs filed an opposition to the motion on August 29, 2025. A hearing on the motion took place on October 20, 2025. On January 12, 2026, the unaffiliated voters filed a petition for a writ of certiorari in the Supreme Court of Maryland. The petition asks the Supreme Court to hear the appeal now, rather than waiting to potentially entertain the appeal after a judgment by the Appellate Court of Maryland. text: Maryland State Board of Elections State Administrator’s Report March 26, 2026 Important Announcements and Meetings Gambling on elections is illegal in Maryland. A person may not make a bet or wager on election results. Despite this prohibition, some platforms, known as prediction markets, are structured differently from traditional gambling sites and are framed as “forecasting” rather than betting. These platforms allow users to trade contracts based on the outcomes of events, including elections. It is important for Maryland residents to understand that even though such platforms are accessible online, participation may still conflict with state law. Engaging in election-related wagering within the State could expose individuals to legal penalties. So just don’t do it. On March 23-25, Election Systems & Software (ES&S) provided demonstrations of the new voting system that is being considered beginning in the 2028 election cycle. This solution was selected through the competitive bid and state procurement process. This is a requirement as part of the state voting system certification process and highlighted the accessible ballot marking device and precinct based tabulator. The demonstration allowed the public to ask questions and submit comments regarding the proposed voting system’s functionality, ease of use, and overall experience. Information on this event was shared on social media, on our website and in a recent press release. Currently, the SBE team is reviewing the questions and comments that were submitted. In preparation of the 2026 Election, we have reviewed and audited the Official Turnout Statistics Reports. During this audit of data query, it was discovered that since 2016, the reports did not have all of the relevant election information. We have worked diligently to recompile the Official Turnout Statistics Reports.

title: Attachment 1_ ExpressVote 3 Usability Report
text: The evaluation is to fulfill the usability testing requirement of the Voluntary Voting System Guidelines (VVSG) and the associated EAC Decision on Request for Interpretation 2013-04 (Usability Testing). The test was conducted from June 1 to July 31, 2023 in the Central Iowa area. Participants from four demographic groups used the ExpressVote 3 in a simulated election. There were at least 8 participants in each group: voters who are blind, voters with low vision, voters with low dexterity, and voters who are non-disabled. Three participants qualified for two demographic groups and evaluated the machines based on their membership in both groups. The election consisted of one test ballot with 11 contests, including:  Federal, state and local contests  Partisan and nonpartisan contests  Single member and multimember contests  Retention races  Constitutional amendments  Referenda and ballot initiatives The test ballot, developed by ES&S, was used to simulate the tasks that users would be asked to perform during a real election. This ballot included 13 tasks that modelled typical ballots from around the country, including:  Voting for a specific name within a list of names  Voting a partial slate in a multimember contest  Skipping elements of a ballot  Write-in voting  Changing a vote after initially selecting it During the usability test, participants were instructed on how to vote and were asked to perform the tasks without assistance. Following the conclusion of the testing, the results were analyzed to determine participants’ effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction using the ExpressVote 3.

Level out of 100 (StdDev: Score) 22) Usability Test Results, 2023 4 ExpressVote 3 2.0 INTRODUCTION 2.1 FULL PRODUCT DESCRIPTION During the usability test, the ExpressVote 3 was evaluated. Designed to present ballots to voters throughout the U.S. and collect voter responses, the ExpressVote consists of a device that accepts an activation card that is either blank or is pre-printed with information that the unit uses to automatically select the ballot if there are more than one ballot programmed on the machine. Once the card is inserted, the unit displays the ballot contests multiple contests per screen or, optionally in assistive mode, voters are presented with one contest per screen. Voters can make their selections and then print the vote summary card after voting is complete. The marked vote summary card is then ejected from the machine to be removed by a voter. The ExpressVote is to be used in federal, state, and local elections and is set up in designated voting locations. The usability testing attempted to simulate these environmental conditions and users’ real-world context of use. 2.2 TEST OBJECTIVES The usability test objectives included:  To assess the effectiveness of the ExpressVote by measuring the abilities of users to successfully complete a ballot.  To assess the efficiency of the product by measuring the average time to complete a voting session.  To assess the user satisfaction of the system by measuring average voter confidence and average voter satisfaction. 3.0 METHOD 3.1 PARTICIPANTS A total of 34 general voters, with a varying mix of backgrounds and demographic characteristics, were selected to participate in the usability test. Participants indicated their demographic group via a question in the Demographics Survey.

The machine then informs the user what the current contest is, how many candidates are available (including a write-in candidate), and the maximum number of candidates that can be selected. title: ES&S EVS 6.5.0.0 Testing Report - FINAL
text: The purpose of these tests was to determine the extent to which the EVS 6.5.0.0 voting system complies with the provisions of the Election Law Article of the Annotated Code of Maryland and the Code of Maryland Regulations (COMAR), Title 33. ES&S applied for State certification in Maryland on March 9, 2026. The contents of an application for certification are defined in COMAR 33.09.03, and include, but are not limited to: ● Identification of the system. ● Overview of the system. ● List of other jurisdictions where the system is used. ● Qualification certification if testing is completed by an independent testing laboratory. ● Copy of certification of the System, if certified by another state. ● Application Fee. COMAR 33.09.03.04 requires the applicant to submit a Technical Data Package, a Business Information Package, anti-bribery and anti-debarment affidavits, as well as voting equipment. These were all submitted. System Description The voting system evaluated by the SBE is called EVS 6.5.0.0. This solution is made by ES&S Voting Systems Inc. of Omaha, Nebraska. An application for testing of the solution by a Voting System Test Laboratory (VSTL) was submitted by ES&S November 1, 2023, to the United States Election Assistance Commission (EAC). Pro V&V (VSTL) accredited by the EAC conducted the testing of EVS 6.5.0.0. The test plan was formally approved on February 13, 2024. Voluntary Voting System Guidelines Version 1.0 (VVSG 1.0) was the standard used for the testing of this solution. EVS 6.5.0.0. was certified by the EAC on July 24, 2024. The list below of components comprises what has been tested by the voting system division of the SBE.

Ballots were hand-marked by the SBE staff to be used in the test. Additionally, ballot activation cards were utilized to mark ballots electronically using the ExpressVote. All ballots marked by hand and electronically were tabulated using precinct and central tabulators. A DS300 precinct tabulator was provided for precinct and early voting simulations. The DS300 is a proprietary scanner with a touchscreen interface. The voter marks his or her ballot with a pen or pencil and feeds it into the scanner. The scanner is programmed with a USB memory device that is not accessible to the voter. When scanned, the ballot is scrutinized, and feedback is displayed to the voter, Election Systems and Software EVS 6.5.0.0 Certification 4/20/2026 Page 5 of 32 MARYLAND STATE BOARD OF ELECTIONS TESTING REPORT – EVS 6.5.0.0 such as notification of overvotes and undervotes, on the LCD – with the voter being given the option to correct his or her ballot. If there are no notifications for review by the voter, the ballot drops into a secure ballot bin, and the voter is shown a message stating that the ballot has been counted. A DS450 central count tabulator was provided for mail-in and Provisional simulations. The DS450 is a proprietary scanner, capable of processing up to 60 ballots a minute. The scanner has a touchscreen interface and is capable of ‘out sorting’ ballots that require scrutiny or adjudication.

title: ES&S EVS 6.5.0.0 Testing Report - FINAL
text: Testing Scope The scope of testing for the proposed voting system encompassed a comprehensive evaluation of system functionality, performance, accuracy, and compliance with applicable regulatory standards. Testing activities began on March 10, 2026, and were completed on Friday, April 17, 2026. The effort included assessment of all major system components, including hardware, software, and supporting infrastructure. In addition, all firmware and hash values of the components provided by ES&S were verified against the trusted hashes provided by the EAC which confirmed authenticity of the product. Election Systems and Software EVS 6.5.0.0 Certification 4/20/2026 Page 6 of 32 MARYLAND STATE BOARD OF ELECTIONS TESTING REPORT – EVS 6.5.0.0 Testing scenarios were designed to simulate pre-election, election day, and post-election activities to ensure full lifecycle reliability. Additionally, the scope included validation of security controls (i.e. system hardening, user access restrictions) and audit capabilities to ensure the integrity of election data throughout all processes. The evaluation for the recommendation of certification was conducted in accordance with Maryland Election Law (Title 9) and COMAR (33), which establish the legal and regulatory framework governing voting system certification within the state. In support of this evaluation, databases provided by ES&S, utilizing Maryland-specific data elements, were used to replicate realistic election conditions. Voting system staff also created new elections within the system to further test configuration flexibility and system responsiveness. As part of the testing process, staff manually and electronically marked over 1,500 ballots to ensure the system could accurately process a high volume of votes under varied conditions. These activities were critical in validating that the system meets statutory and regulatory requirements for accuracy, reliability, and usability. Data outputs generated by the proposed solution were thoroughly evaluated to ensure accuracy, completeness, and proper integration with the SBE systems.

title: ES&S EVS 6.5.0.0 Testing Report - FINAL
text: These activities were critical in validating that the system meets statutory and regulatory requirements for accuracy, reliability, and usability. Data outputs generated by the proposed solution were thoroughly evaluated to ensure accuracy, completeness, and proper integration with the SBE systems. Reports, logs, and exported datasets were reviewed to confirm consistency with expected results and compliance with reporting standards. Integration testing verified that data exchange between the voting system and SBE systems functioned seamlessly without data loss or corruption. Appendix A of this report provides an outline of Maryland Election Law and COMAR and includes an overview of compliance with each regulatory requirement as it pertains to EVS 6.5.0.0. Pursuant to the Annotated Code of Maryland, § 9-102(h)(2), the Maryland Department of Disabilities (MDOD) completed a usability and accessibility review of the proposed solution on Wednesday, April 1, 2026. The SBE received a report from MDOD on Thursday, April 2, 2026, which is included as Appendix B. The report provided by MDOD was also shared with ES&S and the SBE requested and official response to the findings outlined in the report. ES&S did provide a formal response to the findings which is included in this report as Appendix C. Additionally, as part of the Technical Data Package and the application for certification, ES&S provided a Usability and Accessibility report for the ExpressVote 3 which is included as an attached to this test report. The report demonstrates that the ExpressVote 3 meets or exceeds all applicable EAC VVSG 1.0 accessibility standards.

Date: April 23, 2026
To: Maryland State Board Members
From: Jared DeMarinis, State Administrator
Subject: Certification Recommendation for EVS 6.5.0.0.
Pursuant to the Code of Maryland Administrative Regulations 33.09.04.04, I am recommending
certification of EVS 6.5.0.0 and its associated hardware and software to be used in the State of
Maryland.
• EVS software version 6.5.0.0, including several client applications:
ElectionWare version 6.5.0.0.

• DS300 Precinct Tabulator 3.2.0.0
• DS450 Central Tabulator 4.4.0.0
• DS950 Central Tabulator 4.4.0.0
• ExpressVote (3) 4.4.0.0
The Maryland State Board of Elections has undertaken a comprehensive evaluation of the
EVS6500 voting system to determine its suitability for certification and deployment. This
recommendation is grounded in the system’s demonstrated reliability, security, and compliance
with federal standards. Notably, the EVS6500 suite received certification from the U.S. Election
Assistance Commission (EAC) on July 24, 2024, confirming its adherence to the Voluntary
Voting System Guidelines (VVSG) 1.0.
Pursuant to the Code of Maryland Administrative Regulations 33.09.04.05, the State Board of
Elections conducted a series of public demonstrations of the EVS6500 system. These
demonstrations were held simultaneously at three different locations across the state over a three-
day period, from March 23, 2026, through March 25, 2026. This approach allowed for broad
geographic access and enabled voters, stakeholders, and election officials to observe and interact
with the system firsthand. In addition to the in-person demonstrations, a comprehensive video
overview was produced and published on the State Board of Elections website, as well as shared
across official social media platforms.
FAX (410) 974- 2019 Toll Free Phone Number (800) 222-8683 151 West Street Suite 200
MD Relay Service (800) 735-2258 https://elections.maryland.gov Annapolis, Maryland 21401

Public feedback was actively solicited during the in-person demonstrations and also encouraged
at the conclusion of the published video. Feedback pertaining to the proposed voting system was
accepted through April 17, 2026. The response from participants and viewers was
overwhelmingly positive, with many highlighting the system’s ease of use. This feedback played
an important role in validating the decision to recommend the solution for certification.
In addition to public engagement, extensive internal testing was conducted by members of the
Voting System Division over a period exceeding 40 calendar days. This rigorous testing process
included verification of firmware integrity, configuration and definition of election parameters,
and both manual and electronic ballot marking. The system’s tabulation capabilities were
thoroughly evaluated, along with its ability to generate accurate and comprehensive election
reports.
Collectively, these efforts demonstrate that the EVS6500 system meets all necessary technical,
operational and regulatory requirements, supporting its certification for use in the State of
Maryland.
4/20/2026 2

title: Public Citizen Comments on Certification of EVS 6.5.0.0
text: April 22, 2026 Mr. Michael G. Summers, Chairman Mr. Jim Shalleck, Vice Chairman Ms. Victoria Jackson-Stanley Ms. Diane Butler Mr. Eric Bryant Maryland State Board of Elections 151 West Street, Suite 200 Annapolis, MD 21401 Re: Certification of EVS 6.5.0.0 Dear Chair Summers and Members of the Board, On behalf of the members of Public Citizen, I write to you today to urge the Board to pause approval and certification of the new voting system that is under discussion for the state of Maryland. This is not a request we make lightly, but believe this is in the best interest of the voters and the state of Maryland because: Elements of the proposed purchase contract do not meet Maryland election regulations and could expose Maryland’s elections to legal challenges. Touchscreen voting machines under consideration record and tabulate votes from unreadable barcodes, a practice that is less secure than marking ballots by hand, less trusted by voters, and that may invite legal challenges. The proposed system has been built and tested to voting system standards that are more than twenty years old, the 2005 Voluntary Voting System Guidelines (VVSG) 1.0. It is inadvisable to invest this substantial sum of taxpayer dollars in a “new” system that is so profoundly outdated when there are systems available that have been built and tested to more recent 2021 federal voting standards. We elaborate on these points below. Elements of the proposed purchase contract do not meet Maryland election regulations and could expose Maryland’s elections to legal challenges. According to representations made to the press and at public demonstrations, the purchase will include a ballot remaking system from Enhanced Voting. This technology is designed to duplicate ballots received and marked via the internet-based ballot delivery system.

title: Public Citizen Comments on Certification of EVS 6.5.0.0
text: Elements of the proposed purchase contract do not meet Maryland election regulations and could expose Maryland’s elections to legal challenges. According to representations made to the press and at public demonstrations, the purchase will include a ballot remaking system from Enhanced Voting. This technology is designed to duplicate ballots received and marked via the internet-based ballot delivery system. This means that this technology is part of the “voting system,” as defined by the Help America Vote Act of 2002, and therefore must be certified pursuant to Maryland election law. But crucially, the ballot remaking system has not been tested by a federally accredited testing lab and does not meet the performance and test standards established by the Election Assistance Commission, as required in MD Code, Election Law, § 9-102(d)(2)(i) and (ii). If this technology is incorporated into the election system, it could expose Maryland’s elections and election results to legal challenges. Touchscreen voting machines under consideration record and tabulate votes from unreadable barcodes, a practice that is less secure than marking ballots by hand, less trusted by voters, and that may invite legal challenges. The ExpressVote ballot marking devices, included in the proposed equipment package, record votes for tabulation in barcodes. This technology is facing broad opposition and legal challenges because votes recorded in barcodes are unverifiable by the voter. Colorado became the first state in the nation to prohibit the use of barcodes for the recording and tabulation of votes in 2019. In 2024, the Georgia legislature passed legislation that banned barcodes and QR codes for the recording of votes. In March of 2025, an Executive Order issued by the White House sought to end the use of barcodes.

title: Public Citizen Comments on Certification of EVS 6.5.0.0
text: Colorado became the first state in the nation to prohibit the use of barcodes for the recording and tabulation of votes in 2019. In 2024, the Georgia legislature passed legislation that banned barcodes and QR codes for the recording of votes. In March of 2025, an Executive Order issued by the White House sought to end the use of barcodes. Federal courts have held that the Executive Order was not lawful, but questions around the legality of recording and counting votes from barcodes persist. Common Cause New York and the Black Institute are currently suing in New York State, charging that the barcodes violate state law and voter protections. There are other options to provide accessible ballot marking devices that do not record votes in barcodes, including a new device offered from the proposed vendor ES&S. ES&S has developed a device that it is currently marketing in other states to provide accessible ballot marking without the use of unverifiable barcodes. Maryland need not invest in a system dependent on this outdated, unpopular and legally unstable design. The proposed system has been built and tested to voting system standards that are more than twenty years old, the 2005 Voluntary Voting System Guidelines (VVSG) 1.0. It is inadvisable to invest this substantial sum of taxpayer dollars in a “new” system that is so profoundly outdated when there are systems available that have been built and tested to more recent 2021 federal voting standards. Maryland election code requires voting systems be tested by a federally accredited laboratory to meet federally established voting system standards. However, the law overlooks the fact that there are two sets of federally established standards; one adopted in 2005 termed VVSG 1.0, and a set of standards more recently adopted in 2021 termed VVSG 2.0.

title: Public Citizen Comments on Certification of EVS 6.5.0.0
text: Maryland election code requires voting systems be tested by a federally accredited laboratory to meet federally established voting system standards. However, the law overlooks the fact that there are two sets of federally established standards; one adopted in 2005 termed VVSG 1.0, and a set of standards more recently adopted in 2021 termed VVSG 2.0. The system under consideration for certification by the Board of Elections, ES&S’ EVS 6.5.0.0, has been built and tested to the profoundly outdated 2005 VVSG 1.0. There are other options. At present two vendors’ systems are available that meet VVSG 2.0, and several more are in the process of certification to VVSG 2.0. For a taxpayer investment of this size, it would be much more advisable for Maryland to purchase an election system that is not using twenty year-old technology, even if this means leasing equipment in the short term. For these reasons, we urge the Board to withhold certification of the proposed system to address these shortcomings. We welcome your questions and stand ready to provide any additional information or assistance in any way. Thank you for your time and consideration. Respectfully, Robert Joerg Representative, Public Citizen’s Democracy Campaign rjoerg@citizen.org

text: April 22, 2026 Mr. Michael G. Summers, Chairman Mr. Jim Shalleck, Vice Chairman Ms. Victoria Jackson-Stanley Ms. Diane Butler Mr. Eric Bryant Maryland State Board of Elections 151 West Street, Suite 200 Annapolis, MD 21401 Re: Certification of EVS 6.5.0.0 Dear Chair Summers and Members of the Board, We1 write to you today to urge the Board to pause approval and certification of the new voting system that is under consideration for the great state of Maryland. We do not make this request lightly, but believe this is in the best interest of the voters and the state of Maryland because: a) The proposed purchase contract includes elements that do not meet Maryland election regulations and could put Maryland’s elections in jeopardy for legal challenges. b) The touchscreen voting machines under consideration record and tabulate votes from unreadable barcodes, a practice that is less secure than marking ballots by hand, less trusted by voters, and that may invite legal challenges. c) The proposed system has been built and tested to voting system standards 1 Free Speech For People is a non-profit, non-partisan public interest legal organization that works to renew our democracy and our United States Constitution for the people. As part of our mission, we are committed to promoting, through legal actions, secure, transparent, trustworthy and accessible voting systems for all voters. that are more than twenty years old, the 2005 Voluntary Voting System Guidelines (VVSG) 1.0. It is inadvisable to invest this substantial sum of taxpayer dollars in a “new” system that is so profoundly outdated when there are systems available that have been built and tested to more recent 2021 federal voting standards.

title: SEB.comments.certification of 6.5.0.0
text: It is inadvisable to invest this substantial sum of taxpayer dollars in a “new” system that is so profoundly outdated when there are systems available that have been built and tested to more recent 2021 federal voting standards. We elaborate on these points below. a) The proposed voting system may violate Maryland election code, inviting legal challenges to the system and/or to Maryland’s election results. According to representations made to the press2 and at public demonstrations, the purchase will include a ballot remaking system from Enhanced Voting.3 This technology is designed to duplicate ballots received and marked via the internet- based ballot delivery system. This means that this technology is part of the “voting system,” as defined by the Help America Vote Act of 2002,4 and therefore must be certified pursuant to Maryland election law.5 But crucially, the ballot remaking system has not been tested by a federally accredited testing lab and does not meet the performance and test standards established by the Election Assistance Commission, as required in MD Code, Election Law, § 9-102(d)(2)(i) and (ii). If this technology is incorporated into the election system, it could expose Maryland’s elections and election results to legal challenges. b) The proposed system will continue the use of touchscreen ballot marking devices that record votes in unreadable and unverifiable barcodes that is less trusted by voters, and that may invite legal challenges. The ExpressVote ballot marking devices, included in the proposed equipment package, record votes for tabulation in barcodes. This technology is facing broad opposition and legal challenges because votes recorded in barcodes are unverifiable by the voter. 2 Jennifer Franiciotti, “Board of Elections seeking public comment on new voting machines coming to Maryland,” WBALTV, (18, Mar. 2026).

title: SEB.comments.certification of 6.5.0.0
text: The ExpressVote ballot marking devices, included in the proposed equipment package, record votes for tabulation in barcodes. This technology is facing broad opposition and legal challenges because votes recorded in barcodes are unverifiable by the voter. 2 Jennifer Franiciotti, “Board of Elections seeking public comment on new voting machines coming to Maryland,” WBALTV, (18, Mar. 2026). Available at: https://www.wbaltv.com/article/board-of- elections-public-opinion-new-voting-machines-maryland/70782142 3 https://www.enhancedvoting.com/solutions/enhanced-remake/ 4 Public Law 107-252 5 MD Code, Election Law, § 9-102 Colorado became the first state in the nation to prohibit the use of barcodes for the recording and tabulation of votes in 2019.6 In 2024, the Georgia legislature passed legislation that banned barcodes and QR codes for the recording of votes.7 In March of 2025, an Executive Order issued by the White House sought to end the use of barcodes.8 Federal courts have held that the Executive Order was not lawful,9 but questions around the legality of recording and counting votes from barcodes persist. Common Cause New York and the Black Institute are currently suing in New York State, charging that the barcodes violate state law and voter protections. There are other options to provide accessible ballot marking devices that do not record votes in barcodes, including a new device offered from the proposed vendor ES&S. ES&S has developed a device that it is currently marketing in other states10 to provide accessible ballot marking without the use of unverifiable barcodes. Maryland need not invest in a system dependent on this outdated, unpopular and legally unstable design. c) The proposed system has been built and tested to voting system standards that are more than 20 years old, the 2005 Voluntary Voting System Guidelines (VVSG) 1.0, even though more updated technology is available.

title: SEB.comments.certification of 6.5.0.0
text: Maryland need not invest in a system dependent on this outdated, unpopular and legally unstable design. c) The proposed system has been built and tested to voting system standards that are more than 20 years old, the 2005 Voluntary Voting System Guidelines (VVSG) 1.0, even though more updated technology is available. Maryland election code requires voting systems be tested by a federally accredited laboratory to meet federally established voting system standards. However, the law overlooks the fact that there are two sets of federally established standards; one adopted in 2005 termed VVSG 1.0, and a set of standards more recently adopted in 2021 termed VVSG 2.0.11 6 Kevin Collier, “First on CNN: Colorado becomes first state to ban barcodes for the counting of votes over security concerns,” CNN, (16, Sept. 2019). Available at: https://www.cnn.com/2019/09/16/politics/colorado-qr-codes-votes 7 “Georgia governor signs election changes into law,” Associate Press, (7, May 2024). Available at: https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/elections/georgia-governor-brian-kemp-signs-new-election- changes-law-rcna151180 8 https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/03/preserving-and-protecting-the-integrity- of-american-elections/ 9 Julia Shumway, “Federal judge blocks Trump election order, siding with Oregon, Washington,” Oregon Capitol Chronicle, (9, Jan. 2026). Available at: https://oregoncapitalchronicle.com/2026/01/09/federal-judge-blocks-trump-election-order-siding-with- oregon-washington/ 10 https://elections.ny.gov/accessible-voting 11 https://www.eac.gov/voting-equipment/voluntary-voting-system-guidelines The system under consideration for certification by the Board of Elections, ES&S’ EVS 6.5.0.0, has been built and tested to the profoundly outdated 2005 VVSG 1.0.12 There are other options. At present two vendors’ systems are available that meet VVSG 2.0, and several more are in the process of certification to VVSG 2.0.13 For a taxpayer investment of this size, it would be much more advisable for Maryland to purchase an election system that is not using twenty year-old technology, even if this means leasing equipment in the short term. For these reasons, we urge the Board to withhold certification of the proposed system to address these shortcomings.

In the week of April 6, the State Board of Elections was highlighted in the media 18 times over various platforms.

Online: 14

title: State Administrator_s Report- April 23, 2026_
text: We are working to make all of our public facing documents accessible in compliance with the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 Level AA.  Through our Website Accessibility Initiative, we are actively reviewing and converting our existing public-facing electronic documents—such as PDFs—to ensure they are properly structured and fully accessible for those using assistive technologies like screen readers. This commitment aligns with the updated Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act, ensuring that our vital election information and online services are perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust for every voter.

title: State Administrator_s Report- April 23, 2026_
text: SBE has coordinated preparations to provide voting information and materials to incarcerated individuals as required by EL Sec. 1-303.2. We will ship voting packets and posters to DPSCS, Dept. of Juvenile Services, and county detention facilities to arrive by May 2. DPSCS facilities will also stream a video encouraging eligible people to register and vote via inmates’ tablets. SBE is in the process of hiring personnel to collect voting materials from dropboxes installed in DPSCS facilities. We are also raising awareness of voting rights by partnering with DPSCS and the Dept. of Juvenile Services to make voting information available through community, parole, and probation-administering offices, and by participating in DPSCS Reentry Resource Fairs.

title: State Administrator_s Report- April 23, 2026_
text:
The SBE Election Judge Train-The-Trainer program has been completed for the Primary. 51 trainers successfully completed the program. Trainers are in the process of being deployed to their assigned local boards.

LBE Tech training will begin at the end of April. Upon successfully completing training, LBE Techs will be deployed to local boards to provide on-site technical support for the voting system and pollbooks.

title: State Administrator_s Report- April 23, 2026_
text:
Local board logistics meetings have been completed. These meetings allowed local boards to provide key information used in logistics planning and preparation for voting system deliveries.

Ballot drop box deliveries will begin on Monday, May 4th, and will be completed by Friday, May 8th.

title: State Administrator_s Report- April 23, 2026_
text: To improve voter experience, a modification to the drop boxes is underway. The change addresses voter concerns about drop boxes being “locked open”. The modification removes any visual indicators that may falsely suggest that the box is locked while it is accepting ballots.

title: State Administrator_s Report- April 23, 2026_
text: We continue to track election judge recruitment, pay rates, and training schedules and are well situated in preparation for the 2026 Gubernatorial Primary.  To this date, we have received over 1600 responses just through our online interest application. Over 10,000 election judge openings have been reported filled for early voting and election day of the primary and at least eight local boards report staffing at 100% or higher.  We are preparing to visit and evaluate election judge training at the 12 jurisdictions that were not reviewed in the previous election cycle.

title: State Administrator_s Report- April 23, 2026_
text: In collaboration with seven participating LBEs, SBE is providing the Election Day Page program (est. 2019, SB 364) for the Gubernatorial Primary.  The program offers an exciting opportunity for students 14 years old or older to participate in the election process while earning community service credit.  The goals of the program are to encourage the interest of students in the election process, assist election judges, and ensure safe entry and exit of elderly and disabled voters.  SBE makes available materials for communication and training for the LBEs.  While participation is optional, we encourage all LBEs to offer this opportunity to students in their county.  This program not only benefits the students that choose to participate, but the polling places and LBEs as well.  Pages can provide assistance to election judges and voters.

title: State Administrator_s Report- April 23, 2026_

The Maryland Election Administration Education Program (MEAE) is administered by the Maryland

State Board of Elections.  MEAE provides professional development courses and seminars related to topics directly or indirectly related to the election process in Maryland.  We will be conducting one more training session on E-40 Processing before we take a break during the summer.

Ms. McLaughlin will be attending the USPS Postal Conference in May for the 1-day Elections Mail segment.  This is an annual opportunity to meet with high level USPS representatives and with MIV elections workers from around the Country.

The MIV Team will follow up after the election to evaluate the pilot and make a recommendation if this should be an ongoing effort.

Serena Bryson, et al., v. Westley Moore, et al., No. C-02-CV-25-001586 (Cir. Ct. Anne Arundel County). On June 2, 2025, five registered voters unaffiliated with a political party in Maryland served a civil action on the Governor and State Board of Elections. The suit alleges that the registered voters’ electoral rights, granted by the Maryland Constitution, are violated by their inability to vote in state-run, partisan, primary elections. The voters accordingly seek declaratory judgment and an injunction preventing the State from “conducting, organizing or funding State primary elections in which unaffiliated voters are prohibited from voting.” OAG filed a motion to dismiss the complaint on July 30, 2025. Plaintiffs filed an opposition to the motion on August 29, 2025. A hearing on the motion took place on October 20, 2025. On November 14, 2025, the Court granted the motion, dismissing the case in a memorandum opinion. Plaintiffs have appealed the case to the Appellate Court of Maryland. On January 12, 2026, the unaffiliated voters filed a petition for a writ of certiorari in the Supreme Court of Maryland. The petition asks the Supreme Court to hear the appeal now, rather than waiting to potentially entertain the appeal after a judgment by the Appellate Court of Maryland. OAG filed an answer to the petition on January 27, 2026. The Supreme Court denied the petition on March 23, 2026. The Appellate Court of Maryland thereafter scheduled the appeal for routine briefing in that Court. Appellants’ filed their brief on May 6, 2026. OAG will draft and file Appellees’ brief on or before June 5, 2026.

On December 3, 2025, the United States Department of Justice filed suit against the State Administrator of Elections over his response to the department’s multiple demands to disclose Maryland’s unredacted voter registration database. The complaint alleges that the State is in violation of a provision of the Civil Rights Act of 1960 in declining to hand over the unredacted information, as demanded. With the complaint, DOJ filed a motion to compel records pursuant to the Civil Rights Act of 1960. The motion advocates that the Court must dispense with normal process and the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and instead must, in a summary fashion, simply compel production of the voter database. By agreement between the parties, OAG filed a motion to dismiss and an opposition to the motion to compel on January 30, 2026. Two intervening defendants also filed motions to dismiss and oppositions to the motion to compel on the same date. DOJ filed a consolidated response to all the defendants’ filings on February 13, 2026. The defendants filed a reply to the opposition on February 27, 2026. The parties have filed numerous notices of supplemental authority since the motions have been briefed. title: Home Security Guidance May 2026 Board Meeting.docx
text:
Jared DeMarinis Michael Summers, Chairman
State Administrator Jim Shalleck, Vice Chairman
Diane Butler
Katherine Berry
Victoria Jackson-Stanley
Deputy Administrator
Eric Bryant
MARYLAND STATE BOARD OF ELECTIONS
HOME SECURITY GUIDANCE
Issue Date: May 21, 2026
The State Board of Elections issues this guidance for publication and inclusion as a section in the
Summary Guide reaffirming its legal understanding of permissible expenditures.
Home security has become more important in recent years. In 2025 there were politically motivated
home attacks on candidates. Fear of one’s physical safety is reality in today’s political climate. Certain
home security expenses can be personal or have an electoral purpose. The determination of the
purpose for the expense will decide whether campaign funds are permissible.
Maryland law requires campaign funds to be used solely for the purpose of supporting or opposing a
candidate, question, or political committee. See Election Law Article §1101(aa). Moreover, there must
exist a nexus between the expenditure and the candidacy or ballot question to which the expenditure
relates. In other words, the expenditure is permissible if it would not have occurred but for the fact a
candidacy or ballot question is being promoted, supported or opposed. Therefore, expenditures in
support of home security countermeasures would have to have an electoral purpose in order for them to
be permissible. For example, a campaign that installs a home security system for a candidate that has
received threats of harm makes an expenditure that would not have occurred but for the candidacy.
Moreover, the expenditure has a nexus to enhancing the success of the candidacy. As a result of this
analysis, the expenditure for the home security system would be a permissible expenditure. However, if
the home already had a home protection system installed then it would not be because the expenditure
has no bearing on whether the candidate ran for office.
Furthermore, it is permissible for a political party or a legislative party caucus committee to provide
cybersecurity protection for candidate campaigns. The political party can allocate the resources used as
a coordinated in-kind contribution to the campaign in order to keep expenses at a minimum for a small
campaign. Since the expenditures in this scenario would have a campaign purpose, administrative funds
may not be used.
Finally, if campaign funds are used for the procurement of a home security system, it is an asset of the
campaign. When the individual is no longer a candidate for office or closes the candidate committee, this
asset must be disposed of like all of the assets of the committee.
This policy does not, nor cannot, address every instance or possibility for the use of campaign funds to
pay for a home security system. It should be read as non-exhaustive and illustrative guidance.
