text: Jared DeMarinis Michael Summers, Chairman State Administrator Jim Shalleck, Vice Chair Diane Butler Katherine Berry Victoria Jackson-Stanley Deputy Administrator Eric Bryant 2026 Gubernatorial Primary Election Canvass Overview Useful Terms: 1. “Original” ballots - ballots sent to voters by the printing vendor prior to the identification of the vendor error that have been voided in MDVOTERS. 2. “Replacement” ballots - ballots sent to voters by the printing vendor who were issued an “original” ballot to replace that ballot. 3. “Remaining” ballots - ballots sent to voters by the printing vendor after the replacement ballots were sent. 4. “Other” ballots - ballots issued by the local boards of elections, web delivery ballots, and ballots not affected by the vendor error. Background: Due to a vendor error, mail-in ballots sent to roughly 447,000 voters potentially contained the wrong party ballot. To ensure each voter received the correct party ballot, SBE reprinted ballots for all affected voters. The original ballots were voided in the voter registration system. Voided is an operational term that describes the status of a ballot in our voter registration system. It is not a description of the legal status of the ballot. SBE has existing safeguards in place to make sure that only one ballot is counted for each voter. Mail-In Voting is managed by our voter registration system. This system tracks all ballots that are issued to voters. It has safeguards in place to ensure that only one ballot is counted per voter. In order to be counted, or canvassed, a ballot needs to be "received" by scanning the barcode on the voter's return envelopes. If a voter gets a ballot and has a replacement ballot issued, the first ballot is "voided" so it cannot be received into the voter registration system.

title: 2026 Canvass Overview
text: In order to be counted, or canvassed, a ballot needs to be "received" by scanning the barcode on the voter's return envelopes. If a voter gets a ballot and has a replacement ballot issued, the first ballot is "voided" so it cannot be received into the voter registration system. This ensures each voter can only have one ballot counted. Due to the error in printing, all original ballots were voided. This means that operationally, they cannot be scanned and received into the voter registration system and allows the LBE to identify and store these ballots separately. The legal status of these ballots will be determined during canvass, based on guidance provided by the State Board. In addition to voiding the first ballots, SBE included various indicators on the replacement ballots, so that they could be differentiated from the original ballots. Most prominent, the words “Replacement Ballot Inside” was printed on the envelope sent to voters with the ballot packet. On the return envelope, the words “Return Envelope” were printed. There were additional measures taken to ensure (1) replacement ballots could be differentiated from original ballots; (2) that replacement return envelopes could be identified in the event that the flap containing the works “Replacement Envelope” was removed; and (3) that the party of the voter could be identified by the LBE from the envelope to ensure the ballot inside matched the party affiliation. Management of Original and Replacement Ballots: LBE’s were instructed to store “original” mail-in ballots separate from “replacement”, “remaining” and “other” ballots in a secure manner with controlled access. The ballots were to be stored using an organizational process that allowed the LBE to locate a voter’s ballot by name or voter ID.

title: 2026 Canvass Overview
text: Management of Original and Replacement Ballots: LBE’s were instructed to store “original” mail-in ballots separate from “replacement”, “remaining” and “other” ballots in a secure manner with controlled access. The ballots were to be stored using an organizational process that allowed the LBE to locate a voter’s ballot by name or voter ID. Guidance was provided to the LBEs as to how to manage the process of checking “original” ballots to determine if a “replacement” ballot has been received for the voter. (See Original Ballot Review and Processing) Each original ballot was logged in a statewide tracking sheet to facilitate voter communications. SBE sent several emails and text messages to voters who had returned “original” ballots encouraging them to return their “replacement ballots” using this information. The LBEs will be sending postcards to these voters in the next few days. Canvass of Mail-in Ballots: SBE provides LBEs with canvassing guidance for every election. SBE has instructed LBEs that “original” ballots will not be considered for canvass until after the statutory ballot receipt deadline of July 6, 2026 at 10:00 a.m. After this time, “original” ballots for which no “replacement” ballots were received can be canvassed by the LBEs, using guidance provided by SBE. Relevant to the canvass of “replacement” ballots, SBE has historically provided two documents to the LBEs: (1) a Canvassing Scenarios Chart and (2) Canvass Guidance for each election. For this election, SBE did not need to update the Canvassing Scenarios Chart, but did produce a third document to supplement it called Canvass Instructions for Voters Sent Replacement Ballots. This document is to be used for any voter who was sent an “original” and “replacement” ballot.

title: 2026 Canvass Overview
text: For this election, SBE did not need to update the Canvassing Scenarios Chart, but did produce a third document to supplement it called Canvass Instructions for Voters Sent Replacement Ballots. This document is to be used for any voter who was sent an “original” and “replacement” ballot. This document, along with the Canvassing Scenarios Chart, are the technical documents used by the LBEs to determine which ballot to count, in the event two ballots are returned. They were prepared in consultation with subject matter experts from both SBE and the LBEs. The Canvass Guidance was also updated to provide reminders to the LBEs about canvassing “replacement” and “original” ballots. The Canvass Instructions for Voters Sent Replacement Ballots serves two primary purposes. First, it provides a framework for the LBE to determine if the voter returned a replacement ballot. Second, it provides the canvass outcome for each voter’s ballot (i.e. how to count the voter’s ballot). With regard to determining if the “replacement” ballots were returned by the voter, the Canvass Instructions for Voters Sent Replacement Ballots instructs the LBE how to use identifying marks on the ballot and envelope, to determine whether a “replacement” or “original” ballot was returned. In the event that an “original” ballot was returned, it sets forth the process to ensure that the correct party ballot was returned. If an incorrect party ballot was returned, the Canvass Instructions for Voters Sent Replacement Ballots sets out the process to duplicate the contests for which the voter was eligible to vote, so that ballot can be canvassed and only those contests can be counted. Taken together, the Canvass Scenarios Chart and Canvass Instructions for Voters Sent Replacement Ballots provide detailed instructions on how to canvass each voter’s ballot(s).

title: 2026 Canvass Overview
text: Taken together, the Canvass Scenarios Chart and Canvass Instructions for Voters Sent Replacement Ballots provide detailed instructions on how to canvass each voter’s ballot(s). However, they reflect several overarching canvassing situations/outcomes: ● If a voter returns a “replacement” ballot, regardless of whether they returned an “original” ballot or not, that “replacement” ballot should be counted. ● If a voter returns only an “original” ballot, after reviewing it to make sure that it is the correct party ballot, it should be counted. ● If a voter returns only an “original” ballot, and it is the wrong party ballot, there are two possible outcomes. If there are nonpartisan contests, those contests are duplicated onto a new ballot and counted. If there are no nonpartisan contests, the ballot is rejected. ● If a voter returns an “original” ballot and voted a provisional ballot in the polling place, the provisional is counted. ● If a voter returns a “replacement” ballot and voted a provisional ballot in the polling place, the first legally sufficient ballot is counted. Scanning of Ballots during Canvass: “Original” ballots that are scanned during canvass must be scanned and stored separately from “replacement”, "remaining", and the “other” ballots. To facilitate this process, LBEs will have separate tabulators for “original” ballots, as well as separate media to transfer the results into the election management and results system and separate storage bins.

title: GP26 Final Original Ballot Precanvass Management
text: Maryland State Board of Elections Original Ballot Review and Processing Original Ballot Review and Processing I. Definitions A. “Original” ballots - ballots sent to voters by Taylor prior to the identification of the printing error that have been voided in MDVOTERS B. “Replacement” ballots - ballots sent to voters by Taylor who were issued an “original” ballot to replace that ballot. C. “Remaining” ballots - ballots sent to voters by Taylor after the replacement ballots were sent. II. Processes for managing “original” ballots prior to canvass A. Store “original” mail-in ballots separate from “replacement” ballots and “remaining” ballots in a secure manner with controlled access. 1. These ballots should be stored using some organizational process that allows you to locate a voter’s ballot by name or VID. 2. Do not remove the flap on “original” ballots or otherwise process the “original” ballot prior to final canvass. 3. Log these ballots onto the “Voided First Ballot Return Tracking” SBE tracking sheet. Receive in MDVOTERS the “replacement” ballots and “remaining” ballots as soon as they are received by the LBE, in accordance with the law. As “replacement” ballots and “remaining” ballots are returned to the LBE, determine if there is a corresponding “original” ballot. 1. SBE will provide a list daily of all ballots received into MDVOTERS the day before. Using the daily list provided by SBE, by comparing it to the quarantined “original” ballots, identify any “original” ballots for voters who have returned a “replacement” ballot or “remaining” ballot. 2. Keeping those ballots quarantined, separate them from the “original” ballots and securely store them. This ensures that you will not have to review them, prior to final canvass because you have confirmed that the voter has returned another legally sufficient ballot. 3.

title: GP26 Final Original Ballot Precanvass Management
text: Keeping those ballots quarantined, separate them from the “original” ballots and securely store them. This ensures that you will not have to review them, prior to final canvass because you have confirmed that the voter has returned another legally sufficient ballot. 3. Note on the “Voided First Ballot Return Tracking” SBE tracking sheet that a “replacement” ballot or “remaining” ballot was received for that voter. III. Processing for reviewing “original” ballots prior to final canvass A. Pull the “original” ballots that you have identified as not having had a “replacement” ballot or “remaining” ballot returned by the voter. If you have an up-to-date record of these ballots on the “Voided First Ballot Return Tracking” SBE tracking sheet, this can also be used. Manually search each voter in MDVOTERS to determine if they have: 1. Another MIB in received status 2. In person voting credit 3. Provisional Voting Credit C. If a voter has another MIB in received status or in person voting credit, continue to securely store the “original” ballot away from “replacement” ballots and “remaining” ballots and do not send it for canvass. If the voter does not have any other ballot (mail, in person, or provisional), 1. Remove the “original” ballot from quarantine and send this ballot for canvassing. See the 2026 Original Ballot Processing In MDVOTERS document for step by step instructions on how to process these ballots 2. Use the Canvass Instructions for Voters Sent Replacement Ballots to process the ballot for canvass and recommend to the board of canvassers the correct outcome. Note the outcome of every voter on the “Voided First Ballot Return Tracking” SBE tracking sheet, using the following status. 1. Replacement ballot received 2. Voted in Person 3. Voted provisional ballot 4. Original ballot sent to canvass

text: ASSISTANT ATTORNEY GENERAL’S REPORT June 25, 2026 1. California, et al., v. Trump, et al., 1:25-CV-010810 (D. Mass)- On April 3, 2025, nineteen states, including Maryland, filed a civil complaint in the federal district court for the District of Massachusetts against the President, the United States Attorney General, the Election Assistance Commission, and the United States Secretary of Defense. The complaint alleges, amongst seven counts, that the Executive Order imposing certain requirements on the conduct of voter registration and federal elections is unlawful. On April 23, 2025, the defendants moved to consolidate the lawsuit with a second set of lawsuits filed in Washington D.C. that challenged the executive order. The court denied that motion on May 9, 2025. On May 5, 2025, the plaintiff states asked the court for a preliminary injunction to pause implementation of provisions of the Executive Order while the lawsuit was pending. The court granted the preliminary injunction after a hearing. The defendants have appealed the grant of the preliminary injunction to the First Circuit. Separately, on June 13, 2025, the defendants moved to dismiss the complaint. The plaintiff states filed a response in opposition on July 11, 2025. The Court conducted a hearing on the motion on September 4, 2025. On September 17, the Court issued a memorandum opinion and order denying the motion to dismiss. Thereafter, the proceedings were stayed at the government’s request due to the lapse in appropriations for the Department of Justice. That stay lifted when appropriations were reallocated to the Department. On Friday, December 12, 2025, the parties filed cross-motions for summary judgment. The complaint alleges, amongst three counts, that the Executive Order directing the United States Postal Service, Department of Homeland Security, and Department of Justice to take certain actions in relation to mail-in ballots is unconstitutional and illegal. The complaint seeks a declaratory judgment and injunctive relief enjoining Sections 2, 3 and 5 of the Executive Order. On April 14, 2026, the district court granted the parties’ request for an expedited schedule for dispositive motions. A hearing on dispositive motions will be held on June 2, 2026. OAG has worked with SBE staff to draft a factual declaration to support the plaintiff- state’s motion for summary judgment. On June 21, 2026, the district court issued an order granting the government’s motion to dismiss in part. The district court ruled that the plaintiff states’ complaint was not ripe as to elections taking place after this November’s general election. It therefore dismissed the complaint as it related to elections beyond the November 2026 general election. The remainder of the complaint, and the government’s motion, remains pending before the Court. 3. Serena Bryson, et al., v. Westley Moore, et al., ACM-REG-2151-2025 (App. Ct. of Md.) The voters accordingly seek declaratory judgment and an injunction preventing the State from “conducting, organizing or funding State primary elections in which unaffiliated voters are prohibited from voting.” OAG filed a motion to dismiss the complaint on July 30, 2025. The complaint alleges that election officials in Maryland are violating the National Voter Registration Act (“NVRA”) by failing to make reasonable efforts to remove eligible voters from the voter registration database. In support of that allegation, the complaint cites estimated population statistics and compares them to SBE’s reported voter registration totals. On January 12, 2026, The Democratic National Committee moved to intervene in the case as a defendant. The plaintiffs (RNC, Md. GOP, and voters) did not oppose the motion to intervene. OAG, on behalf of SBE, took no position on the motion. The motion remains pending before the Court. OAG filed a motion to dismiss the complaint on January 30, 2026. The local boards of elections, through their counsel, also filed motions to dismiss on the same date. On June 25, 2026 Assistant Attorney General’s Report February 2, 2026, the Court granted the pending motion to intervene, permitting the DNC to participate in the case as a defendant. By stipulation between the parties, the plaintiffs filed an amended complaint removing the local boards of elections from the case. Both defendants filed renewed motions to dismiss the amended complaint on April 24, 2026.

Mr. Wilson asks the Court to void and destroy all Washington County Republican Primary ballots and have them reprinted and recertified with his opponent absent from them. OAG on behalf of the State Board promptly filed a motion to dismiss the petition. Mr. Wilson opposed the motion and OAG filed a reply. We are writing to seek clarification on your comments regarding the counting of any

As you know, thousands of incorrect ballots for the opposite party were mailed to
Maryland voters. While correct replacement ballots were subsequently mailed to

arrived, and may not have followed through with sending in the corrected ballots.

will not be cast “because of the board’s extensive communication with voters.” While
we hope this is the case, we are asking that you clarify the process for reviewing
these ballots that ensures these incorrect votes – where voters have in fact cast votes
for candidates in the opposite party – are not counted.
For example, if you receive a ballot from a registered Republican who submitted the
incorrect ballot of Democratic candidates for office, but did not submit their correct
ballot, what is the process for invalidating the erroneous ballot?
We understand this is a busy time for the Board of Elections, as the review of mail-in
ballots begins today. But, as we know you will agree, it is imperative to our
democracy that our citizens have confidence in the transparency and integrity of our
elections. We look forward to your timely response to this important request.
Sincerely yours,
Delegate Jason Buckel Delegate Jesse Pippy

in every election. Every mail-in ballot issued is tracked in the secure

title: House_Admin_Response_06122026
text: Jared DeMarinis Michael Summers, Chairman State Administrator Jim Shalleck, Vice Chairman Diane Butler Katherine Berry Victoria Jackson-Stanley Deputy Administrator Eric Bryant June 12, 2026 Chair Bryan Steil Ranking Member Joseph Morelle Committee on House Administration Committee on House Administration 1309 Longworth Office Building 1216 Longworth Office Building Washington, DC 20515 Washington, DC 20515 Dear Chair Steil, Ranking Member Morelle and Committee members: I write in response to Chair Steil’s letter dated May 26, 2026. Before I address your and the committee’s individual concerns and questions, it is important to reiterate that mail-in voting is legal and constitutional. Mail-in voting is nonpartisan. Mail-in voting is a safe, secure and verified method of voting. No fraudulent ballots were sent out. To state otherwise leads to the creation of an environment for mis- and disinformation to confuse voters, sow distrust in election results and undermine the electoral process. As the State Administrator and staff of the Maryland State Board of Elections (SBE), we serve as the definitive and trusted source for all electoral information within the State. It is absolutely vital that the public, including concerned stakeholders like yourself, possess a clear and accurate understanding of the detailed, often complex, and statutorily defined administrative processes that govern election law. We recognize the current information environment presents significant challenges. Narratives surrounding mail-in voting and sensational social media posts with no factual basis frequently misconstrue, miscategorize, or misinterpret the law or certain rights. This often leads to the proliferation of misinformation—inaccurate information spread unintentionally—and disinformation—false information spread with the intent to deceive. The integrity of our elections hinges on our ability to counteract this trend. We are committed to ensuring that those seeking accurate, truthful, and legally correct answers receive them in a timely manner from the official, trusted source.

title: House_Admin_Response_06122026
text: This often leads to the proliferation of misinformation—inaccurate information spread unintentionally—and disinformation—false information spread with the intent to deceive. The integrity of our elections hinges on our ability to counteract this trend. We are committed to ensuring that those seeking accurate, truthful, and legally correct answers receive them in a timely manner from the official, trusted source. Our goal is to demystify the election process and restore public confidence through transparency and factual clarity. Being transparent about election administration is vital to building trust. Transparency must apply when issues affecting voters and other stakeholders occur. Once the vendor mail-in ballot issue was reported to the Maryland State Board of Elections (SBE), we took decisive and corrective actions immediately. These corrective measures were to ensure the integrity of mail-in voting and allow the voter the maximum time with the correct party ballot to cast an informed vote. FAX (410) 974- 2019 Toll Free Phone Number (800) 222-8683 151 West Street Suite 200 MD Relay Service (800) 735-2258 https://elections.maryland.gov Annapolis, Maryland 21401 This office engaged in a robust targeted voter outreach campaign to potentially affected voters. Over 400,000 postcards and emails were sent. Additionally, over 100,000 text messages were sent, and I have made myself available to the press. Our office works diligently to protect Marylanders’ constitutional right to vote and their constitutional right to vote by mail as well. Here are the answers to your specific questions. 1. What specific mechanical, digital, or procedural error within the third-party vendor's system caused the mail-in ballot error? Generally speaking, there was a vendor issue with the application of the party affiliation code to the ballot and ballot envelope used to data match the two pieces together for an individual voter. As a result, some voters received the wrong party ballot.

title: House_Admin_Response_06122026
text: What specific mechanical, digital, or procedural error within the third-party vendor's system caused the mail-in ballot error? Generally speaking, there was a vendor issue with the application of the party affiliation code to the ballot and ballot envelope used to data match the two pieces together for an individual voter. As a result, some voters received the wrong party ballot. Based on information provided by our vendor at that time, the vendor could not accurately identify individual affected voters. 2. What protocols does the SBOE have in place to audit and verify the accuracy of mail-in ballots prior to distribution, and does the SBOE plan to alter these protocols given this incident? To be clear, this error was not a result of SBE’s failure to audit and verify the accuracy of mail-in ballots prior to distribution. SBE continuously audits all aspects of operations, including management of the voter registration database and voter requests for mail-in ballots, under the direction of staff dedicated to the task. The accuracy of the list of mail-in voters requesting a ballot by mail complies with State laws and regulations. Moreover, our internal protocols have been effective in producing accurate instructions and information for our vendor to implement for execution. Since the issue occurred with the vendor, SBE required additional safeguards and quality control review of the code for the production and packaging of replacement ballots for the June 23 Primary. Additionally, our Director of Mail-In Voting was onsite at the vendor’s facility to observe and confirm accuracy. 3. How many of the approximately 565,000 original ballots are estimated to be incorrect? As SBE has previously stated, over 447,000 replacement ballots were sent. Again, the vendor was unable to accurately identify the voters affected by the error. Print at home (web-delivered) ballots were not impacted. 4.

title: House_Admin_Response_06122026
text: How many of the approximately 565,000 original ballots are estimated to be incorrect? As SBE has previously stated, over 447,000 replacement ballots were sent. Again, the vendor was unable to accurately identify the voters affected by the error. Print at home (web-delivered) ballots were not impacted. 4. If a voter returns only the original, incorrect mail-in ballot, is the entire ballot discarded, such that none of the voter’s selections are counted? In accordance with the policies formally adopted by SBE during its June 9, 2026 special meeting, original ballots timely received from voters who do not submit any other ballot will be processed after the mail-in ballot receipt deadline of July 6 at 10am. If the original ballot meets all legal requirements for mail-in voting and is the correct party ballot style for the voter, it will be counted. If a voter returns only an original ballot for the incorrect party, the local board of elections will duplicate the voter’s votes for any nonpartisan contests on that ballot onto the ballot style that the voter should have voted and scan that ballot. If there are no nonpartisan contests on an original, incorrect ballot from a voter who did not return any other ballot, the original ballot will be rejected in its entirety. 5. What corrective actions or contractual changes is the SBOE implementing to prevent similar vendor errors in the future? Prior to the replacement ballots being mailed, a SBE representative went to the facility to do a walk- through where the vendor demonstrated areas for improvement in their process in order to ensure ballots were being prepared and released properly. As part of the remedial process, SBE worked with the vendor to implement additional quality control measures for future mail-in ballot printing.

title: House_Admin_Response_06122026
text: As part of the remedial process, SBE worked with the vendor to implement additional quality control measures for future mail-in ballot printing. SBE is currently reviewing its contract with the vendor to identify areas of noncompliance and ensure that the vendor has a plan in place to comply with all contractual terms for the general election. The vendor has set out several specific action items that they will undertake to ensure acceptable performance under the current contract and to avoid similar errors in the future. In the coming months, SBE will conduct internal lessons learned as we do after every election. The lessons learned will include an in-depth analysis of the mail-in voting process. Additionally, we will be compiling a new Request for Proposals (RFP) for a future mail-in ballot printing vendor for the State of Maryland. SBE is required to follow Maryland state procurement laws as it pertains to selection of vendors. The current contract with our mail-in ballot vendor is in its final option year. 6. Has the SBOE launched a formal internal investigation into this incident? If yes, what are the preliminary findings? The primary focus of SBE has been to ensure the vendor issue has been remedied and to get replacement ballots to voters in a timely fashion, so that they can return them for the primary election. As part of the remedial process, SBE has requested information from the vendor about the cause of the issue, as well as steps taken to ensure that similar issues do not occur in the future. Again, SBE will perform a lessons learned analysis and anticipates additional requests for information and communication with the vendor to ensure a full understanding of both the cause and the remedy implemented by the vendor to prevent future issues. 7.

title: House_Admin_Response_06122026
text: Again, SBE will perform a lessons learned analysis and anticipates additional requests for information and communication with the vendor to ensure a full understanding of both the cause and the remedy implemented by the vendor to prevent future issues. 7. How will the SBOE ensure a similar incident does not occur prior to the November general election? SBE continues to engage the vendor to ensure that the root cause of this issue was identified and corrected, such that it will not occur again in the future. Since the coding issue was related to party affiliation, this particular issue cannot occur in the general election. Even though this particular coding issue cannot occur in the general election, SBE insists that additional quality control measures are implemented to avoid any incidents for the general election. We are scheduled to begin printing of the 2026 General Election ballot no later than Thursday, September 3, 2026. Thank you for the opportunity to alleviate any of your concerns regarding the conduct of Maryland’s 2026 Primary Election. Sincerely, Jared DeMarinis State Administrator of Elections

title: Letter From LWV - Question
text: Date May 21, 2026 To: State Board of Elections Administrator Jared DeMarinis CC: Chairman Michael Summers; Maryland State Board of Elections From: Nikki Tyree, Executive Director, League of Women Voters of Maryland Linda T. Kohn, President, League of Women Voters of Maryland Subject: Urgent need to resolve voter confusion around mail-in ballots The League of Women Voters of Maryland (LWVMD) is concerned and disappointed by the lack of clarity and transparency in the process for counting mail-in ballots for the June 23rd primary election. Upon learning about the tainted batch of ballots that went out to voters, LWVMD closely monitored communications from the State Board of Elections. It was our understanding, as well as the voters who reached out to us, that these ballots would ultimately be voided. This has been stated in press releases directing voters to “destroy” their first ballot and stating that only the replacement ballot will be counted. However, with yesterday's press release becoming public, voters have been thrown into mass confusion about which ballots will exactly be counted. If the State Administrator considered this problem serious enough to replace all 400,000 mail-in ballots, why is there now hesitancy to lay out a clear, expedited, and understandable path to solving it? As such, the League of Women Voters of Maryland must call on the State Board of Elections to void all of the mail-in ballots that were included in that tainted batch. We do not do this lightly, but rather with a priority on ensuring full election integrity and voter confidence in the electoral process. SBE’s plans to handle this like any other time they replace a ballot are not sufficient for this situation.

title: Letter From LWV - Question
text: We do not do this lightly, but rather with a priority on ensuring full election integrity and voter confidence in the electoral process. SBE’s plans to handle this like any other time they replace a ballot are not sufficient for this situation. In those cases, an individual initiates the action to request a replacement ballot because they mis-marked the ballot or misplaced it, perhaps; it is not common or widespread. However, in this case, the SBE is initiating the action on behalf of hundreds of thousands of voters. It is a large-scale problem that confuses voters. LWVMD understands that some of these ballots have already been returned, so time is of the essence. By leaving Maryland voters unsure which ballots will be counted, the State Board has opened the state to widespread confusion and the belief that our elections lack integrity. It is now known that incorrect ballots, including possibly party ballots being sent to unaffiliated voters, are leaving voters to question whether the ballots being returned are legitimate. By instituting a strict policy of voiding these ballots, voters can move forward knowing that only the correct ballots will be counted. Furthermore, given this political climate, voter confidence needs to be of the utmost concern. It is not enough for agency leaders or a select few to know the ins and outs; rather, each voter should be able to be sure of the process during this troubling time. Already, this confusion has taken hold, with many Local Boards of Elections unable to report exactly what will happen to the first ballot. LWVMD has heard it said that the first ballots will “generally” not be counted; that the first ballots will be voided; and, worst of all, that some LBEs do not even know their status.

title: Letter From LWV - Question
text: Already, this confusion has taken hold, with many Local Boards of Elections unable to report exactly what will happen to the first ballot. LWVMD has heard it said that the first ballots will “generally” not be counted; that the first ballots will be voided; and, worst of all, that some LBEs do not even know their status. Beyond that, numerous voters have reached out to the League to express concern that emails sent by SBE appear to be scams. LWVMD understands that some of these ballots have already been returned. As the leading voting rights organization in Maryland, we would never call for disenfranchising voters, but rather exhaust all possible avenues to reach these voters and instruct them on how to vote the replacement ballots. This can be done by using text-to-cure technology to alert voters that their ballots have been received, but they need to vote for the replacement, and by sending additional postcards, texts, emails, and phone calls, or any combination. In the League’s opinion, SBE is functionally issuing multiple live ballots and expecting the voter to figure it out. That is not a way to ensure the integrity of the election and confidence in the results (by both voters and candidates). We cannot allow voters to be unsure of the process, distrust it, or feel so anxious that they choose not to vote. That is how voters get disenfranchised. The League respects that these are difficult and unprecedented times. More than that, we greatly appreciate and value our partnership with the State Board of Elections and the Administrator. However, our mission is clear: empowering voters and defending democracy. LWVMD believes that SBE is falling short, and LWVMD will use all available resources and tools to advocate for the Maryland voter.

title: Oversight Letter - MD SBOE Mail-In Ballots
text: May 26, 2026 Jared DeMarinis State Administrator Maryland State Board of Elections 151 West Street, Suite 200 Annapolis, MD 21401 Dear Administrator DeMarinis: The Committee on House Administration (Committee) has broad oversight of federal elections.1 Oversight of federal elections is critical to safeguard the integrity of America’s electoral system. Your office, the Maryland State Board of Elections (SBOE), recently reported a vendor error that resulted in many voters receiving the wrong party ballot.2 This issue merits careful attention and assurance that it will not recur. The Committee is therefore seeking information from the Maryland State Board of Elections.

title: Oversight Letter - MD SBOE Mail-In Ballots
text: Your office, the Maryland State Board of Elections (SBOE), recently reported a vendor error that resulted in many voters receiving the wrong party ballot.2 This issue merits careful attention and assurance that it will not recur. The Committee is therefore seeking information from the Maryland State Board of Elections. On May 5, 2026, your office announced that 565,639 voters requested mail-in ballots for the 2026 primary election.3 Following the first phase of mailing ballots, a grave error was discovered: a printing and mailing vendor distributed incorrect party ballots to an unknown number of voters for the June 23 primary election.4 Because the number of incorrect ballots could not be determined, the SBOE announced it would preemptively send replacement ballots to every voter who requested a mail-in ballot.5 1 Rules of the House of Representatives, Rule X (K) Committee on House Administration. 2 Maryland State Board of Elections, Press Statement, Maryland State Board of Elections Addresses an Error with Mail-In Ballots (May 15, 2026), available at https://elections.maryland.gov/press_room/documents/2026/Mail_in_Ballot_Press_Statement.pdf. 3 Maryland State Board of Elections, Press Statement, Maryland State Board of Elections Announces 565,639 Voters Have Requested Mail-In Ballots for the 2026 Primary Election (May 5, 2026), available at https://elections.maryland.gov/press_room/documents/2026/SBE_Total_Mail_In_Ballots_Requested_May_2026.pdf 4 See Robert Lang, Maryland State Board of Elections to replace incorrect mail-in ballots after printing glitch, WBAL NEWS RADIO 1090 & FM 101.5 (May 19, 2026), available at https://www.wbal.com/state-unveils-ballot- replacement-plan. 5 Maryland State Board of Elections, Press Statement, Maryland State Board of Elections Addresses an Error with Mail-In Ballots (May 15, 2026), available at https://elections.maryland.gov/press_room/documents/2026/Mail_in_Ballot_Press_Statement.pdf.

title: Oversight Letter - MD SBOE Mail-In Ballots
text: Administrator DeMarinis May 26, 2026 Page 2 of 3 While the SBOE is taking precautions to void the initial batch of ballots, distributing over half a million additional replacement ballots risks creating immense logistical strain and potentially undermines public confidence in the nation’s elections.6 These systemic errors raise concerns over pre-distribution auditing and state oversight of critical third-party contractors. Based on this information, the Committee is concerned about the administration, tracking, and security of Maryland’s mail-in voting processes, and whether adequate safeguards are in place for the upcoming general election. To assist the Committee’s oversight of this matter, please provide the following information as soon as possible, but no later than June 9, 2026: 1. What specific mechanical, digital, or procedural error within the third-party vendor's system caused the mail-in ballot error? 2. What protocols does the SBOE have in place to audit and verify the accuracy of mail-in ballots prior to distribution, and does the SBOE plan to alter these protocols given this incident? 3. How many of the approximately 565,000 original ballots are estimated to be incorrect? 4. If a voter returns only the original, incorrect mail-in ballot, is the entire ballot discarded, such that none of the voter’s selections are counted? 5. What corrective actions or contractual changes is the SBOE implementing to prevent similar vendor errors in the future? 6. Has the SBOE launched a formal internal investigation into this incident? If yes, what are the preliminary findings? 7. How will the SBOE ensure a similar incident does not occur prior to the November general election? If you have any questions, please contact the Committee at 202-225-8281. Thank you for your prompt attention to this matter.

title: State Administrator's Report- June 25, 2026
text: Maryland State Board of Elections State Administrator’s Report June 25, 2026 Important Announcements and Meetings On June 6, Jared DeMarinis met with the leadership of the League of Women Voters. He addressed the mail-in ballot issue and upcoming preparations for the Primary Election. On June 8, Jared attended a Cardin Center event on Democracy for the Future. The Empowering Secure Elections lab was there to promote our new app, GoVoteMD. GoVoteMD is a voter information app designed to help Marylanders connect with reliable information about upcoming elections and voting opportunities. Dr. Natalie Scala, who leads the Empowering Secure Elections lab demonstrated the app, and helped attendees explore how it can serve as a resource for voters. On June 17, the Maryland Department of Disabilities reviewed and tested the new proposed voting system, in particular the new proposed ballot marking device. The Maryland State Board of Elections continues to remain open and transparent as we navigate the 2026 Gubernatorial Election. We have always and continue to follow all laws and regulations regarding running an election, including mail-in ballot procedures, voter list maintenance, canvassing practices, and document retention. Currently, there is some confusion about the commencement of the final mail-in ballot canvass. The 10th day after the election is July 3. Because July 3 is a Federal Holiday, no canvasses will be held and the legal deadline moved to July 6. The canvassing process requires notice be given publicly directly to the chairman of the county central committee of each party, candidates who are not a part of a political party and also to the State Administrator. This is to be posted prominently on the LBE’s website. All of the canvassing sessions, deliberations and proceedings are open to the public and media.

title: DOJ_Response_07132026
text: Jared DeMarinis Michael Summers, State Administrator Chairman Jim Shalleck, Vice Katherine Berry Deputy Administrator Chairman Diane Butler Victoria Jackson-Stanley Eric Bryant Harmeet K. Dhillon Assistant Attorney General Civil Rights Division U.S. Department of Justice 950 Pennsylvania Ave. NW - RFK Washington, DC 20530 Sent by email to William.Mohrman@usdoj.gov Dear Assistant Attorney General Dhillon: I write in response to your letter dated July 7, 2026. You requested a letter in response informing “how the state of Maryland intends to ensure it is complying with” the list maintenance mandates of the NVRA, HAVA, Title III of the Civil Rights Act of 1960, and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 at both the state and local level. As the State Administrator and staff of the Maryland State Board of Elections (SBE), we serve as the definitive and trusted source for all electoral information within the State. It is absolutely vital that the public possess a clear and accurate understanding of the detailed, often complex, and statutorily-defined administrative processes that govern election law. Narratives surrounding voter registration, especially those circulating on various social media platforms, frequently misconstrue the law or certain rights. This often leads to the proliferation of misinformation—inaccurate information spread unintentionally—and disinformation—false information spread with the intent to deceive. The integrity of our elections hinges on our ability to counteract this trend. Under Maryland law, the State Administrator, local boards, and election directors each perform voter registration list maintenance duties. Under Maryland Code, Election Law Article § 3-501, election directors in Maryland’s counties and in Baltimore City have authority to remove voters from the registration list upon their request and upon learning of their loss of eligibility.

title: DOJ_Response_07132026
text: Under Maryland law, the State Administrator, local boards, and election directors each perform voter registration list maintenance duties. Under Maryland Code, Election Law Article § 3-501, election directors in Maryland’s counties and in Baltimore City have authority to remove voters from the registration list upon their request and upon learning of their loss of eligibility. Election Law § 3-502(b)-(c) charges the appropriate election official with sending a confirmation notice upon learning that a voter may have moved, while § 3-502(d)-(e) give election directors responsibility for updating or removing records in accordance with the NVRA and State laws. Section § 3-504 describes the following roles:  The State Administrator secures records of deaths, convictions, and name changes from State and federal agencies;  The local boards receive jurisdiction-specific cuts of this information, as well as obituaries and reports of destruction of residences within their jurisdictions; and  Election directors send confirmation notices and remove voters from the FAX (410) 974- 2019 Toll Free Phone Number (800) 222-8683 151 West Street Sui MD Relay Service (800) 735-2258 https://elections.maryland.gov Annapolis, Maryland Department of Justice response letter July 13, 2026 Page 2 of 3 registration list when statutorily-required conditions are met. In addition, Chapters 6 and 7 of Title 33, Subtitle 5 of the Code of Maryland Regulations (COMAR) elaborate on responsibilities of the State Board and State Administrator, and local boards and election directors, in the voter registration list maintenance program. Provisions include, for example, that under COMAR § 33.05.06.06, the State Board receives reports from the jury commissioner; the State Administrator delivers county-specific information to local boards; and election directors communicate with voters and update or cancel their registration records.

title: DOJ_Response_07132026
text: Provisions include, for example, that under COMAR § 33.05.06.06, the State Board receives reports from the jury commissioner; the State Administrator delivers county-specific information to local boards; and election directors communicate with voters and update or cancel their registration records. Under COMAR § 33.05.07.01(B), election directors mail nonforwardable specimen ballots to all registered voters in their jurisdictions as part of the State’s process to identify individuals who may have become ineligible by reason of a change of address. COMAR § 33.05.07.04 requires election directors to act as soon as reasonably possible to update records in the statewide voter registration list. Maryland voter registration list maintenance procedures are dictated by state law, which derive from NVRA requirements. In general, the NVRA requires that:  State programs make a reasonable effort to remove the names of ineligible voters by reason of death or change of residence, 52 USC § 20507(a)(4);  State programs be uniform, nondiscriminatory, and not result in removal of registered voters solely by reason of failure to vote, 52 USC § 20507(b);  States not remove a registrant on grounds of change of address unless they confirm, or fail to respond to a confirmation notice and do not vote in two general elections for Federal office after receiving a confirmation notice, 52 USC § 20507(d)(1); and  State programs must be completed not later than 90 days before a primary or general election for Federal office, 52 USC § 20507(c)(2)(A). Maryland procedures for voter registration list maintenance are set forth in the Election Law Article, Title 3, Subtitle 5, and COMAR Title 33, Subtitle 5, Chapters 6 and 7. Maryland’s list maintenance processes are generally explained on the State Board of Elections Website: https://elections.maryland.gov/voter_registration/list_maintenance.html.

title: DOJ_Response_07132026
text: Maryland procedures for voter registration list maintenance are set forth in the Election Law Article, Title 3, Subtitle 5, and COMAR Title 33, Subtitle 5, Chapters 6 and 7. Maryland’s list maintenance processes are generally explained on the State Board of Elections Website: https://elections.maryland.gov/voter_registration/list_maintenance.html. Furthermore, Maryland is a member of the Electronic Registration Information Center (ERIC) and follows the coalition’s bylaws and the procedures set forth in its Membership Agreement, both of which may be reviewed and downloaded at the following URL: https://ericstates.org/wp-content/uploads/documents/ERIC-Bylaw- MA-FINAL.pdf. As summarized on the Voter Registration List Maintenance section of our website, “Each ERIC member shares their voter registration data along with data provided by each Department of Motor Vehicles. This allows the data to be matched with member states and against the Social Security Administration’s death records and the National Change of Address (NCOA) program through the U.S. Postal Service. Maryland receives 5 reports from ERIC: in-state duplicate records, death notifications, in-state address changes, cross-state address changes and a report from NCOA regarding address updates.” The State Administrator sends county-specific cuts of ERIC data to local boards and election directors to take appropriate action, in accordance with standard procedures.

Without exhaustion, we highlight here key provisions that guarantee compliance with NVRA requirements for voter registration list maintenance: Department of Justice response letter July 13, 2026 Page 3 of 3  Election Law Article § 3-502(c) requires election directors who receive notice of a move outside their jurisdiction to send a confirmation notice, and § 3- 502(d) prohibits removal of a voter who receives this notice unless the voter confirms their move, or fails to respond and to vote in the two general elections following issuance of the confirmation notice.  COMAR § 33.05.07.01(C) requires that confirmation mailings and subsequent actions to remove voters or place them in inactive status must be completed at least 90 days before an election.  Election Law Article § 3-504(a)(1) requires the State Department of Health to report deaths to the State Administrator. Under § 3-504(a)(2) the State Administrator also must seek arrangements that provide access to Social Security Administration death notices, while local boards are empowered to make arrangements to receive change of address information from approved sources under § 3-504(b)(4).

title: DOJ_Response_07132026
text: Under § 3-504(a)(2) the State Administrator also must seek arrangements that provide access to Social Security Administration death notices, while local boards are empowered to make arrangements to receive change of address information from approved sources under § 3-504(b)(4). When an election director receives a report of death from one of these sources or an obituary or other reliable report, the election director requests confirmation if appropriate, and cancels registration for deceased voters in accordance with provisions in § 3-504(c).  COMAR § 33.05.06.05(A) further specifies that election directors cancel registration immediately upon receiving a report of a voter’s death from a state vital statistics agency, and § 33.05.06.05(B) requires them to send a confirmation letter when a death report comes from another credible source.  Election Law Article § 1-201 provides that the purposes of the State’s election laws include fair and equitable treatment of all voters and assurance that all qualified persons may register. The right to vote is a sacred right that has been expanded through sacrifices of many before us. It is a privilege and honor to work in this field empowering individuals to make their voices heard. The State Board works diligently to ensure that every eligible Marylander can register to vote in accordance with federal and State laws. And as referenced above, election officials in Maryland continue that diligent work to maintain up to date voter rolls. Improper cancellation leads to disenfranchisement of an eligible voter. That is why it is a detailed process. It must be certain. Maryland’s process errs on the side of removing any doubt in the cancellation before potentially disenfranchising a voter.

title: LVW Questions Reply 6.26.26
text: Jared DeMarinis Michael Summers, Chairman State Administrator Jim Shalleck, Vice Chairman Diane Butler Katherine Berry Deputy Administrator Victoria Jackson-Stanley Eric Bryant June 26, 2026 League of Women Voters of Maryland 121 Cathedral St #2B Annapolis, MD 21401 Dear Ms. Tyree and Ms. Kohn, Thank you for providing questions in connection with the State Board of Elections’ June 9, 2026 meeting. We write to respond to the inquiries you sent to us on June 8, 2026. 1) Will voters who send in only the first ballot have an opportunity to cure a ballot as needed, given that they are being held until the end of canvassing? • The issuance of the replacement ballot provided them an opportunity to cure any deficiencies on the original ballot. The local boards of elections will contact voters who have a deficiency on the replacement ballot in order to cure. 2) We want transparency on the outcomes of the process, specifically: how many first ballots were received with no replacement ballot; how many of those were counted/rejected and, if rejected, why; how many first and second ballots were received from the same voter. Is there a process in place to record all this information? • As SBE has previously stated, over 400,000 replacement ballots were sent. It was unclear how many ballots were impacted by the printing error. • SBE created a manual tracking system for original ballots, as well as processing guidelines to ensure ballots are tracked, accounted for and recorded. • SBE and the LBEs are manually tracking and recording all original ballots received and marking them when the same voter has returned a replacement ballot. This tracking is being updated each day in addition to giving voters credit for returning their replacement ballot in the registration database.

title: LVW Questions Reply 6.26.26
text: This tracking is being updated each day in addition to giving voters credit for returning their replacement ballot in the registration database. It is not possible to accept receipt of two ballots for one individual in our voter registration database. • The canvass disposition of the original ballots will be available. • Further details about canvass were finalized at the June 9 State Board Meeting. Meeting materials are available on SBE’s website. FAX (410) 974- 2019 Toll Free Phone Number (800) 222-8683 151 West Street Suite 200 MD Relay Service (800) 735-2258 https://elections.maryland.gov Annapolis, Maryland 21401 League of Women Voters of Maryland June 26, 2026 Page 2 of 4 3) Is there an expectation of the volume of provisional ballots? How many are expected, and how will that affect the timing and resource needs for canvassing? The reasons for requiring a provision ballot should be identified, including whether the voter chose to no longer vote by mail due to the replacement issue. • SBE has not received any voter feedback that indicated a significant increase in provisional voting volume. However, SBE and the LBEs are prepared to accommodate surges. After the 2024 Election Cycle, which saw unprecedented provisional voting, SBE and local boards plan for elevated levels of provisional voting that surpass historical trends, to ensure flexible ability to accommodate needs. Each provisional ballot is and always has been assigned a code corresponding to the reason the voter is completing this kind of ballot. For 2026, there are new reason codes for those that vote provisionally due to having previously requested a mail-in ballot.

title: LVW Questions Reply 6.26.26
text: Each provisional ballot is and always has been assigned a code corresponding to the reason the voter is completing this kind of ballot. For 2026, there are new reason codes for those that vote provisionally due to having previously requested a mail-in ballot. This will give insightful information that we can use to educate voters further in future elections and also consider any changes to our Maryland processes. • SBE notified voters that they also have the opportunity to cancel their request to receive a mail-in ballot by submitting a signed request to election officials no later than June 18 at 6pm. Voters who submitted timely requests to cancel a mail-in ballot were able to vote regular ballots at in-person voting locations. 4) How will holding first ballots received and an increase in the number of provisional ballots affect the timing of canvassing and preliminary results? Are there measures being discussed if canvassing has to go beyond July 6th? • The time necessary to canvass ballots will depend on how many voters return their replacement ballots. SBE provided guidance to the LBEs on how to manage and review original ballots prior to canvass to expedite processing necessary to canvass original ballots. Local boards are tracking their efforts and SBE is monitoring the tracking of incoming mail-in ballots. • SBE will also monitor the canvass schedules provided by the LBEs and consider any barriers to local certification, completion of risk limiting audits, and state certification which is currently scheduled for July 23.

title: LVW Questions Reply 6.26.26
text: Local boards are tracking their efforts and SBE is monitoring the tracking of incoming mail-in ballots. • SBE will also monitor the canvass schedules provided by the LBEs and consider any barriers to local certification, completion of risk limiting audits, and state certification which is currently scheduled for July 23. We have asked that LBEs provide SBE with details regarding estimated certification timelines as we approach the July 6 final scheduled local certification day. 5) Is the BoE getting more inquiries by phone or email than has typically occurred in prior elections? • SBE has sent a significant amount of email and text communications, as well as postcards, to voters to educate them about replacement ballots. After each email blast, there has been an uptick in customer service. Thanks to the efforts of SBE staff, all emails are generally League of Women Voters of Maryland June 26, 2026 Page 3 of 4 answered within 24 hours and most answered in a matter of just hours. • The overall phone and email contact volume is fairly consistent with comparable past election cycles. • As in past election years, SBE set up a call center to handle incoming calls from voters. Between its debut in March 2026 and June 25, 2026, there were 22,021 total incoming calls to SBE, the majority of which were answered by call center agents. • From January 1, 2026 through June 25, 2026, SBE received a total of 4,941 emails to its Absentee, Info, and State Board of Elections addresses. 6) Do you anticipate any challenges to recounts due to the replacement ballots? • It is not possible to answer this question, without the contests being decided. Recount processes are set by law, with regard to the margin of victory and methods permitted.

title: LVW Questions Reply 6.26.26
text: Recount processes are set by law, with regard to the margin of victory and methods permitted. The same laws that govern recounts in past elections will govern recounts in this election. 7) With what legal basis are the LBE’s able to count the replacement ballots? If counting the first ballot received is the current law, and this is a state- initiated action rather than a voter-initiated one, what legal guidelines allow state and local election boards to disregard the first ballot, even if it is correct? • SBE has reviewed the entirety of the Election Law, as it relates to this situation and determined that replacement ballots can be counted as the first legally sufficient ballot. Additionally, the State Board approved canvassing guidance with particular updates pertaining to original ballots at the June 9, 2026 meeting. 8) How are ballots from the first batch being quarantined? How are they being separated out from the replacement ballots? How many people have access to these ballots? • LBEs distinguish the original and replacement ballots from one another as they are received by scanning unique bar codes on envelopes and oaths. Additional security features assist in distinguishing original ballots from the replacements. • SBE instructed LBEs that original ballots must be stored separately from “replacement” ballots and other ballots in a secure manner with controlled access. Precise storage methods and staff access vary from LBE to LBE. • Ballot storage and retrieval systems have been established at every LBE. • LBE employees who have access to sensitive systems and voter information undergo background checks, receive regular training on security and privacy, and are subject to regular peer and supervisory audits of their work.

League of Women Voters of Maryland June 26, 2026 Page 4 of 4 9) If a voter does vote the replacement ballot, how is the first ballot found and destroyed, or is the plan to run all first batch ballots? • Ballot storage and retrieval systems have been established at every LBE involving alphabetizing and sorting strategies. SBE has released specific instructions regarding quarantine and subsequent evaluation for which original ballots need to be considered in the final canvass. • No ballots - regardless if they are being canvassed - are being “destroyed”. • SBE and LBEs follow the retention schedule of 22 months for all election records and documents. Retention includes all ballots received. • To be clear, local boards will not canvass original ballots from voters who return replacement ballots. Page 3 Maryland State Board of Elections State Administrator’s Report July 23, 2026 Clear Ballot Automated Audit The automated tabulation audit, performed by Clear Ballot, verifies the accuracy of our tabulating systems. In the first phase of the audit, local boards exported 100% of ballot images scanned during Early Voting (EV), on Election Day (ED), and canvassed during the first Mail-in Ballot canvass (MIB1). Without any knowledge of the vote totals, Clear Ballot conducts their independent tabulation of the results. Once Clear Ballot’s tabulation was completed, SBE staff exchanged the results reports created by our voting system. Clear Ballot created five different comparison reports comparing their own tabulation results and number of ballots cast with the SBE reports. Any differences greater than 0.5% would require further investigation. Phase 1 reports were provided to all local boards prior to their certification showing: 1. That Clear Ballot tabulated the same number of ballots as was tabulated by our voting system. 2. Any differences in the results between the two systems are less than 0.5%. 3. Clear Ballot's tabulation verified the accuracy of the voting system's results. Phase 2 repeats the above process with all remaining ballots scanned during the final Mail-in Ballot (MIB2) and Provisional canvasses (PROV). Final comparison reports will be finished and provided to local boards prior to the state certification.
